uni-mbbs-anaesthesia-radiology.title: MBBS Clinical · Anaesthesia & Radiology
uni-mbbs-anaesthesia-radiology.description: Anaesthesia and radiology for MBBS students and interns: pre-anaesthetic assessment, airway skills, local anaesthetic safety, chest X-ray interpretation in words and choosing the right imaging safely. A study companion for MBBS students: it does not replace supervised clinical training or a licence.

steps.title: Focus
steps.body: Previous anaesthetics and complications (personal/family — e.g., malignant hyperthermia), airway problems, cardiorespiratory reserve (can you climb two flights of stairs?), OSA symptoms, reflux, drugs (anticoagulants, antiplatelets, diabetes drugs incl. steps.body: I healthy · II mild systemic disease · III severe systemic disease · IV severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life · V moribund, not expected to survive without the operation · VI brain-dead organ donor. 'E' added for emergency.

steps.title: Bedside tests
steps.body: **Mallampati** (patient sitting, mouth open, tongue out, no phonation): class I soft palate, fauces, uvula, pillars visible → class IV only hard palate visible. Mouth opening (inter-incisor gap), thyromental distance, neck extension, jaw protrusion, dentition, beard, obesity, OSA. No single test is reliable; combine and plan.

steps.title: Plan
steps.body: Anticipated difficult airway → senior anaesthetist, difficult-airway trolley, awake techniques considered, front-of-neck access plan.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Doing Mallampati with the patient lying or phonating; ignoring a history of difficult intubation.

steps.title: Manoeuvres
steps.body: Head tilt–chin lift (no c-spine injury suspected) or jaw thrust (suspected c-spine injury); suction secretions; oropharyngeal airway (size: incisors to angle of jaw; only if no gag reflex) or nasopharyngeal airway (tolerated with gag; caution in suspected base of skull fracture); bag-valve-mask with two-person technique if needed; call for help early.

steps.body: Inserting an OPA in a patient with an intact gag (vomiting); poor mask seal; not calling for help.

steps.title: Common adult principles (check local guideline)
steps.body: Many guidelines use about: solids/light meal 6 h, breast milk 4 h (infants), clear fluids 2 h before elective anaesthesia (some newer guidance allows clear fluids closer in selected patients). Emergency patients are treated as full stomach (rapid sequence induction).

steps.title: Medications

courses.title: Local anaesthesia & procedural safety
courses.summary: Local anaesthetic pharmacology, maximum dose calculations, LA systemic toxicity and safe sedation.
outcomes: Learners can convert % solution to mg/mL
Learners can calculate a maximum lidocaine volume
Learners can recognise LA systemic toxicity and order the response
Learners can list monitoring needs for procedural sedation

scenes.text: A student asks why lidocaine stings and why adrenaline is added.
Sodium channels.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body: Local anaesthetics block voltage-gated sodium channels from inside the neuron, stopping action potential propagation; small, unmyelinated fibres (pain, temperature) block first. Amides (lidocaine, bupivacaine) are metabolised by the liver; esters by plasma cholinesterase.

steps.title: Adrenaline
steps.body: Vasoconstriction slows absorption → longer action, less bleeding, higher safe dose. Traditional teaching avoided it in end-arteries (digits, penis); current evidence suggests it's usually safe in digits in healthy patients, but follow local policy.

steps.title: Infection
steps.body: LA works poorly in infected (acidic) tissue.

activity.prompt: Classify the local anaesthetic.

story.title: How much lidocaine can I use?

scenes.text: A 60 kg patient needs a large laceration repair.
Know the maximum before you draw up.

steps.title: Converting %
steps.body: x% solution = x g per 100 mL = **10x mg/mL**. So 1% = 10 mg/mL; 2% = 20 mg/mL; 0.5% = 5 mg/mL.

steps.title: Commonly quoted maxima (check local formulary)
steps.body: Lidocaine plain ~3 mg/kg (max about 200 mg per many references); lidocaine with adrenaline ~7 mg/kg. Bupivacaine ~2 mg/kg. Use lean body weight in obesity, reduce in elderly/frail, cardiac/hepatic disease.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: 60 kg × 3 mg/kg = 180 mg plain lidocaine. 1% = 10 mg/mL → 18 mL maximum.

activity.prompt: A 50 kg patient. Maximum plain lidocaine 3 mg/kg. Using 1% lidocaine (10 mg/mL), what is the maximum volume?

scenes.text: During a large-volume block, the patient says her lips tingle and she feels strange, then becomes agitated.
Stop injecting.

steps.title: Features
steps.body: CNS: perioral tingling, metallic taste, tinnitus, light-headedness, agitation, seizures, coma. Cardiovascular: arrhythmias, hypotension, bradycardia, cardiac arrest (bupivacaine particularly cardiotoxic).

steps.title: Response
steps.body: Stop injecting, call for help, airway with 100% oxygen, control seizures (benzodiazepine per protocol), **IV lipid emulsion** per LAST protocol, advanced life support if arrest (prolonged resuscitation may be needed), report incident.

steps.title: Prevention
steps.body: Calculate maximum dose, aspirate before injecting, incremental injection, ultrasound guidance, monitoring with IV access.

activity.prompt: Order the LAST response.
items: Stop injecting local anaesthetic

Maintain airway and give 100% oxygen
Treat seizures per protocol
Give IV lipid emulsion per protocol

Document and report the incident

scenes.text: A shoulder reduction in casualty needs procedural sedation.

steps.title: Before
steps.body: Consent, fasting status considered, ASA, airway assessment, two trained staff (one dedicated to sedation/monitoring), resuscitation equipment, suction, oxygen, reversal agents.

steps.title: During & after
steps.body: Continuous SpO2, ECG, BP, capnography where available, level of sedation; titrate small doses; recover until baseline with discharge criteria and written advice.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Operator also giving sedation alone; no capnography; discharge before return to baseline.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Before you look
steps.body: Patient details, date, projection (PA vs AP — AP magnifies the heart), position (erect/supine). **RIPE:** Rotation (clavicle heads equidistant from spinous processes), Inspiration (about 6 anterior or 10 posterior ribs), Picture (whole lung fields), Exposure (vertebrae just visible behind heart).

steps.title: ABCDE read
steps.body: **A**irway (trachea central), **B**reathing (lungs, pleura), **C**ardiac (size — cardiothoracic ratio < 0.5 on PA, borders), **D**iaphragm (contour, free air), **E**verything else (bones, soft tissue, lines and tubes).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling cardiomegaly on an AP film; missing lines/tubes; not reviewing areas such as apices and behind the heart.

activity.prompt: Order a systematic chest X-ray read.
items: Check patient details, date and projection
Assess quality: rotation, inspiration, picture, exposure
Airway: trachea and bronchi
Breathing: lungs and pleura
Cardiac: size and borders
Diaphragm and below
Everything else: bones, soft tissues, lines and tubes
Review areas and compare with old films

scenes.text: Your tutor shows five films and describes them aloud.
Match the description to the diagnosis.

steps.title: Descriptions
steps.body:
- **Pneumothorax:** visible lung edge with no lung markings beyond.
- **Pleural effusion (erect):** homogeneous opacity at the base with a meniscus, blunted costophrenic angle.
- **Consolidation:** airspace opacity with air bronchograms.
- **Lobar collapse:** volume loss — shift of fissures/trachea/mediastinum towards the opacity; e.g., left lower lobe collapse 'sail sign' behind heart.
- **Pulmonary oedema:** bat-wing perihilar shadowing, Kerley B lines, upper-lobe diversion, effusions.

steps.title: Shift tells volume
steps.body: Mediastinal shift away = large effusion/tension pneumothorax (mass effect); towards = collapse/pneumonectomy (volume loss).

steps.title: Supine films
steps.body: Pneumothorax may show only a deep sulcus sign; effusions layer as a haze.

scenes.text: An NG tube was placed for feeding; the nurse asks if it can be used.
Misplaced NG feeding into the lung is a 'never event'.

steps.title: NG tube
steps.body: First-line check per policy: aspirate pH (commonly ≤ 5.5 suggests gastric placement). If pH not confirmatory → X-ray: tube follows the oesophagus down the midline, **bisects the carina**, crosses the diaphragm in the midline and the tip is below the left hemidiaphragm. Never use 'whoosh test'.

steps.title: Others
steps.body: ET tube tip ~ 5 cm (range commonly 3–7) above the carina; central venous catheter tip near the cavo-atrial junction; check for pneumothorax after central line insertion; chest drain position.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Seeing a tube in the abdomen and assuming it's in the stomach without tracing its full course; feeding before confirmation.

scenes.text: Six imaging requests arrive. Are they the right test?

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Common first choices
steps.body:
- Gallstones/RUQ pain: **ultrasound**.
- Suspected stroke/acute head injury: **non-contrast CT head**.
- Renal colic: **non-contrast CT KUB** (ultrasound in pregnancy/young).
- Suspected PE: CT pulmonary angiography (after clinical probability/D-dimer as appropriate).
- Spinal cord compression/cauda equina: **MRI**.
- Fracture: **X-ray** first (two views).

steps.title: Ultrasound
steps.body: No ionising radiation — first choice in pregnancy and children where it answers the question.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Ordering CT for everything; skipping clinical assessment; vague requests.

activity.prompt: Choose the best first imaging.

items.text: Suspected renal colic in a non-pregnant adult

options: Ultrasound or MRI without contrast as appropriate

quiz.q: Acute head injury with risk factors

scenes.text: A 26-year-old woman needs a CT abdomen; she's not sure if she's pregnant.
ALARA: as low as reasonably achievable.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body: **Justification** (benefit > risk), **optimisation** (ALARA: lowest dose that answers the question), **dose limitation** (for staff). Women of reproductive age: ask about pregnancy and test when relevant before abdominal/pelvic imaging with ionising radiation; urgent life-saving imaging is not withheld.

steps.title: Relative doses
steps.body: A chest X-ray is a very small dose; CT abdomen is many times greater (roughly hundreds of chest X-rays). Children are more radiosensitive.

steps.title: Staff
steps.body: Time, distance, shielding; lead aprons, dosimeter badges.

activity.prompt: Order the steps before abdominal CT in a woman of reproductive age.
items: Confirm the clinical question and justification

Perform a pregnancy test where indicated

If CT still needed, optimise protocol and document discussion

scenes.text: A patient with a pacemaker and a patient with poor kidney function are booked for scans.
Safety screening prevents disasters.

steps.title: Iodinated contrast (CT)
steps.body: Ask about previous reactions, asthma/atopy, renal function (eGFR) per local policy, metformin guidance per local policy, hydration. Anaphylaxis can occur — resuscitation equipment and adrenaline available.

steps.title: MRI safety
steps.body: Strong magnet: screen for pacemakers/ICDs (some are MR-conditional), cochlear implants, metallic foreign bodies (especially intraocular — welders), aneurysm clips, neurostimulators, pregnancy considerations, claustrophobia. Projectile risk from ferromagnetic objects (oxygen cylinders!). Gadolinium caution in severe renal impairment.

steps.title: Never
steps.body: Never take a ferromagnetic oxygen cylinder or trolley into the MRI room.

steps.body: Patient identity; clinical history and examination findings; specific clinical question; relevant bloods (e.g., creatinine, inflammatory markers); pregnancy status; allergies; contrast/MRI safety; urgency; your name and contact.

steps.body: No clinical question; missing renal function; unclear urgency; illegible contact.

lessons.title: The brachial plexus, built step by step

scenes.text: A 22-year-old falls off a bike and lands on his shoulder, head forced away from it.
In casualty his arm hangs by his side, rotated inwards, the palm facing backwards.
Which part of the plexus was stretched? You can answer it once you can build the plexus.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Roots → trunks → divisions → cords → branches
steps.body:
The plexus forms from the **ventral rami of C5–T1**.

- **Roots** (C5–T1) lie between scalenus anterior and medius.
- **Trunks**: upper (C5–6), middle (C7), lower (C8–T1) — in the posterior triangle of the neck.
- **Divisions**: each trunk splits into anterior and posterior divisions behind the clavicle.
- **Cords** (named by relation to the 2nd part of the axillary artery): **lateral** (anterior divisions of upper + middle), **medial** (anterior division of lower), **posterior** (all three posterior divisions).
- **Terminal branches**: musculocutaneous (lateral cord), ulnar (medial cord), median (lateral + medial roots), axillary and radial (posterior cord).

steps.title: Memory frame
steps.body: Anterior divisions supply **flexor** compartments; posterior divisions supply **extensor** compartments. So every nerve from the posterior cord (axillary, radial, thoracodorsal, subscapular) serves the back of the limb or shoulder.

steps.title: Solved example · Which roots does the median nerve carry?
steps.body:
Step 1: median = lateral root (lateral cord) + medial root (medial cord).
Step 2: lateral cord = C5, C6, C7; medial cord = C8, T1.
Step 3: median nerve therefore carries **C5(6)–T1** fibres — clinically mainly C6–T1.

This is why a lower-trunk lesion weakens the thenar muscles (T1) even though the median nerve itself is intact.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying cords are named by their relation to the clavicle — it is the **axillary artery**.
- Forgetting that the long thoracic nerve (C5–7) comes from the **roots**, not a cord.
- Mixing the suprascapular nerve (from the upper trunk) with the subscapular nerves (from the posterior cord).

activity.prompt: Match each nerve to where it arises in the brachial plexus

quiz.q: Cords of the brachial plexus are named by their relation to the
quiz.why: The lateral, medial and posterior cords are named by their position around the second part of the axillary artery.

quiz.q: Which nerve arises from the posterior cord?
quiz.why: The posterior cord gives the upper and lower subscapular, thoracodorsal, axillary and radial nerves.

quiz.q: The upper trunk is formed by
quiz.why: The upper trunk is C5 + C6; the middle trunk is C7; the lower trunk is C8 + T1.

quiz.q: Winging of the scapula after mastectomy suggests injury to the
quiz.why: The long thoracic nerve supplies serratus anterior, which holds the scapula against the chest wall; it runs on the medial wall of the axilla and is at risk in axillary surgery.

scenes.text: The ortho OPD has four patients with different arm injuries.
One has wrist drop, one a claw hand, one cannot oppose the thumb, one has a flat shoulder.
Sort each sign to the nerve that explains it.

steps.title: The big four peripheral nerve lesions
steps.body:
- **Axillary** (fracture surgical neck of humerus, shoulder dislocation): loss of abduction 15–90° (deltoid), flattened shoulder, numb 'regimental badge' patch over lower deltoid.
- **Radial** (fracture shaft of humerus in the spiral groove): **wrist drop**, loss of finger extension at MCP joints; triceps usually spared because its branches arise above the groove.
- **Median** at the wrist (carpal tunnel): thenar wasting, loss of opposition, sensory loss over the lateral 3½ digits (palmar side). At the elbow: also loss of flexion of index finger — the 'pointing finger' / hand of benediction on trying to make a fist.
- **Ulnar** at the wrist or elbow: **claw hand** (hyperextended MCP, flexed IP joints of ring and little fingers), interossei wasting, positive Froment's sign.

steps.title: The ulnar paradox
steps.body: A lesion at the **elbow** paralyses flexor digitorum profundus to the ring and little fingers too, so the IP joints flex *less* — clawing is milder than with a lesion at the wrist. The more distal the lesion, the worse the claw.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the radial nerve injury in the spiral groove paralyses triceps — usually it does not.
- Calling the 'hand of benediction' an ulnar sign — on attempted fist-making it is median (proximal lesion).
- Forgetting that sensation over the anatomical snuffbox is the superficial radial nerve.

quiz.why: The radial nerve lies in the spiral (radial) groove on the back of the humeral shaft.

quiz.q: Carpal tunnel syndrome typically spares sensation over the thenar eminence because
options: the palmar cutaneous branch passes superficial to the flexor retinaculum
the ulnar nerve supplies the thenar skin
the radial nerve supplies the thenar skin

quiz.why: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve leaves before the tunnel and runs over the retinaculum, so palm sensation is preserved.

quiz.q: Clawing is more marked when the ulnar nerve is cut at the wrist than at the elbow because
options: FDP to the medial fingers is still working
the median nerve is also cut
quiz.why: With a wrist lesion FDP (innervated higher up) still flexes the IP joints strongly, so the claw is worse — the ulnar paradox.

scenes.text: The biker from lesson 1 is now in the ward; you are the intern.
Work through history, examination and the likely lesion.
Know when to call the senior and the surgeon.

steps.title: Erb's palsy (upper trunk, C5–6)
steps.body:
Mechanism: excessive increase in the angle between neck and shoulder (fall on the shoulder, difficult delivery with traction on the head).

Paralysed: deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, biceps, brachialis, brachioradialis, supinator.

Posture — **'waiter's tip'**: arm adducted (deltoid/supraspinatus lost), medially rotated (infraspinatus lost), elbow extended (biceps/brachialis lost), forearm pronated (biceps/supinator lost). Sensory loss over the lateral arm and forearm.

steps.title: Klumpke's palsy (lower trunk, C8–T1)
steps.body:
Mechanism: arm forcibly pulled upward (grabbing a branch while falling, breech delivery with arm above head), or a cervical rib / Pancoast tumour.

All intrinsic hand muscles weak → **claw hand** of all fingers, sensory loss along the medial forearm and hand. If T1 sympathetic fibres are involved: **Horner's syndrome** (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis) on the same side.

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: Any brachial plexus injury after high-energy trauma needs urgent senior review: rule out cervical spine injury and vascular injury (subclavian/axillary artery) first. Nerve conduction and MRI guide whether surgical exploration is needed.

s0.text: Day 1. The 22-year-old is stable. His right arm is adducted and medially rotated with the elbow extended. What do you check first?

choices.label: Pulses, cervical spine and a full neurovascular exam of the limb
choices.feedback: Correct — trauma priorities first, then the nerve. A vascular injury is the emergency.

choices.label: Order a nerve conduction study right away
choices.feedback: Nerve conduction studies are not useful in the first days; secure the airway, spine and vessels first.

s1.text: Radial pulse is present. Shoulder abduction and elbow flexion are absent; hand grip is normal. Sensation is lost over the lateral arm. Where is the lesion?

choices.label: Upper trunk (C5–C6) — Erb's palsy
choices.feedback: Yes: deltoid, spinati, biceps and brachialis are C5–6; the hand (C8–T1) is spared.

choices.label: Lower trunk (C8–T1)
choices.feedback: A lower-trunk lesion spares the shoulder and elbow and affects the hand.

choices.label: Radial nerve in the spiral groove
choices.feedback: That would give wrist drop, not loss of abduction and elbow flexion.

s2.text: You also look at his eyes. Both pupils are equal, no ptosis. What does that tell you?

choices.label: T1 sympathetic outflow is spared, which fits an upper-trunk lesion
choices.feedback: Right — Horner's syndrome would suggest a lower root (T1) avulsion close to the cord, a worse prognosis.

choices.label: He must have a brain injury
choices.feedback: Equal pupils and no ptosis are reassuring here, not a sign of brain injury.

s3.text: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

choices.label: Refer to the orthopaedic / plastic-hand team, splint and start physiotherapy to keep joints mobile
choices.feedback: Good. Early referral; electrodiagnosis at about 3 weeks; surgery is considered if there is no recovery.

choices.label: Reassure and discharge with no follow-up
choices.feedback: Plexus injuries need specialist follow-up; delayed repair has worse outcomes.

end.text: Well managed: trauma priorities, correct localisation (Erb's, C5–6), check for Horner's, timely referral and physiotherapy.

quiz.why: Erb's palsy from an upper-trunk lesion gives the adducted, medially rotated arm with an extended elbow and pronated forearm.

quiz.why: Preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head leave the cord at T1; lower-trunk/T1 root injury can cause Horner's.

options: lower trunk of the brachial plexus
quiz.why: The lower trunk (C8–T1) arches over the first rib near the lung apex.

quiz.why: Biceps is the strongest supinator; with biceps and supinator paralysed the unopposed pronators win.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — axilla and cubital fossa walk-through

scenes.text: In the dissection hall, the examiner points to the axilla and then the cubital fossa.
'Name the walls, then the contents, in order.'
Put the structures in the right sequence and then tick off your revision tasks.

steps.title: The axilla
steps.body:
A pyramid-shaped space between arm and chest wall.

- **Apex** (cervico-axillary canal): bounded by clavicle, first rib and upper border of scapula.
- **Anterior wall**: pectoralis major and minor, clavipectoral fascia.
- **Posterior wall**: subscapularis, teres major, latissimus dorsi.
- **Medial wall**: serratus anterior over the upper ribs.
- **Lateral wall**: intertubercular groove of the humerus.
- **Contents**: axillary artery and vein, cords and branches of the brachial plexus, axillary lymph nodes (anterior, posterior, lateral, central, apical), fat.

steps.title: The cubital fossa
steps.body:
A triangular hollow in front of the elbow. Boundaries: line between the epicondyles above, **pronator teres** medially, **brachioradialis** laterally; floor of brachialis and supinator; roof of deep fascia reinforced by the bicipital aponeurosis, with the median cubital vein superficial to it.

Contents from **medial to lateral**: median nerve, brachial artery (dividing into radial and ulnar arteries), tendon of biceps, radial nerve (deep, under brachioradialis). Memory: 'My Bottom Tastes Rich' .

steps.title: Why it matters clinically
steps.body: The bicipital aponeurosis protects the brachial artery and median nerve during venepuncture of the median cubital vein. Blood pressure is auscultated over the brachial artery just medial to the biceps tendon.

activity.prompt: Arrange the contents of the cubital fossa from MEDIAL to LATERAL

Brachial artery
Biceps tendon
Radial nerve

options: musculocutaneous nerve (lateral cutaneous nerve of forearm)
questions.why: The musculocutaneous nerve continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

questions.q: Case: after a supracondylar fracture a child cannot flex the tip of the index finger or the thumb IP joint but has normal skin sensation. Which nerve?
questions.why: The anterior interosseous branch of the median nerve is purely motor (FPL, lateral FDP, pronator quadratus); the 'OK sign' fails.

options: Both true; reason does not explain

questions.why: Pectoralis minor lies in the anterior wall.

questions.why: Pushing against a wall makes the medial border of the scapula lift off when serratus anterior is weak.

options: avulsion of the T1 root near the spinal cord
a lesion of the lateral cord
questions.why: Horner's means the T1 sympathetic outflow was injured — a proximal (preganglionic) root injury with poorer prognosis.

courses.title: Histology · Tissues You Must Recognise
courses.summary: General histology in words: epithelia, connective tissue, muscle, nerve, cartilage and bone — with the 'spotter' clues examiners look for and the clinical relevance of each tissue.
outcomes: Learners can classify epithelia and name a site for each
Learners can distinguish the three muscle types and cartilage types by their features
Learners can identify common spotters from a written description
Learners can link histology to disease (metaplasia, osteoporosis)

scenes.text: A 50-year-old smoker's bronchial biopsy shows flat layered cells instead of ciliated columnar cells.
The pathologist calls it squamous metaplasia.
To understand it, you first need to know what the airway is supposed to look like.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
Epithelium is classified by **number of layers** (simple, stratified, pseudostratified) and **shape of the surface cells** (squamous, cuboidal, columnar).

- **Simple squamous**: alveoli, endothelium, mesothelium — diffusion and filtration.
- **Simple cuboidal**: thyroid follicles, kidney tubules — secretion/absorption.
- **Simple columnar**: stomach, intestine (with brush border and goblet cells in the intestine).
- **Pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells**: trachea and bronchi — 'respiratory epithelium'. All cells touch the basement membrane, but nuclei are at different heights.
- **Stratified squamous non-keratinised**: oesophagus, vagina, cornea. **Keratinised**: skin.
- **Transitional (urothelium)**: bladder, ureter — dome-shaped umbrella cells that flatten on stretching.

steps.title: Metaplasia
steps.body: Metaplasia is a reversible change of one adult cell type into another better able to withstand stress: respiratory to squamous in smokers; squamous to intestinal-type columnar in the lower oesophagus with chronic acid reflux (Barrett's oesophagus) — a precursor of adenocarcinoma.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling pseudostratified epithelium 'stratified' — every cell rests on the basement membrane.
- Forgetting that transitional epithelium looks different when the bladder is full versus empty.

activity.prompt: Match the epithelium to a typical site

quiz.why: Respiratory epithelium is pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells.

quiz.q: Barrett's oesophagus is an example of
quiz.why: Squamous epithelium changes to intestinal-type columnar epithelium — metaplasia.

quiz.q: Umbrella cells are a feature of
quiz.why: Large superficial dome-shaped umbrella cells characterise urothelium.
The oesophagus resists abrasion with non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium.

lessons.title: Lab: Spotter sort — muscle and cartilage

scenes.text: Ten slides, one minute each, at the spotting exam.
You have only your eyes and the features you remember.
Sort each feature to the tissue it identifies.

steps.title: Three muscle types
steps.body:
- **Skeletal**: long cylindrical multinucleated fibres, nuclei at the **periphery**, cross-striations.
- **Cardiac**: branching fibres, one or two **central** nuclei, striations, **intercalated discs** (gap junctions + desmosomes).
- **Smooth**: spindle-shaped cells, single central cigar-shaped nucleus, no striations.

steps.title: Three cartilage types
steps.body:
- **Hyaline**: glassy matrix with type II collagen, chondrocytes in lacunae (cell nests), perichondrium present — trachea, costal cartilage, articular surfaces (no perichondrium on articular cartilage).
- **Elastic**: elastic fibres in the matrix — pinna, epiglottis, auditory tube.
- **Fibrocartilage**: dense type I collagen bundles with rows of chondrocytes, **no perichondrium** — intervertebral disc, pubic symphysis, menisci.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying cardiac muscle is multinucleated with peripheral nuclei — that is skeletal muscle.
- Saying fibrocartilage has perichondrium — it does not.

activity.prompt: Sort each spotter clue to the tissue

quiz.why: They join cardiac myocytes end to end.

quiz.q: The intervertebral disc's annulus fibrosus is made of

quiz.why: Elastic cartilage allows the epiglottis to bend and spring back.

quiz.q: Type II collagen is characteristic of
quiz.why: Hyaline and elastic cartilage contain type II collagen; bone, tendon and skin are type I.

lessons.title: Lab: Bone histology and a fracture case

scenes.text: A 68-year-old woman falls on an outstretched hand and fractures her distal radius.
Her DXA scan later shows low bone density.
What is happening inside her bone at the microscopic level?

steps.title: Compact bone
steps.body: The unit is the **osteon (Haversian system)**: concentric lamellae around a central (Haversian) canal containing vessels and nerves. Osteocytes sit in lacunae linked by canaliculi. **Volkmann's canals** run transversely, connecting Haversian canals. Interstitial lamellae fill gaps between osteons; circumferential lamellae line the outer and inner surfaces.

steps.title: Bone cells
steps.body:
- **Osteoblasts** (from mesenchymal cells) lay down osteoid and start mineralisation.
- **Osteocytes**: osteoblasts trapped in matrix; sense mechanical load.
- **Osteoclasts**: large multinucleated cells from the monocyte–macrophage lineage, sitting in resorption bays (Howship's lacunae), with a ruffled border.

In **osteoporosis** bone mass is reduced but the bone that remains is normally mineralised; trabeculae thin and lose connections, so fractures of the wrist, vertebrae and hip follow minor falls.

steps.title: When to see a professional
steps.body: Fragility fractures after a minor fall in older adults should prompt evaluation for osteoporosis and fall prevention by a physician.

s0.text: A 68-year-old has a Colles' fracture after tripping at home. In histology terms, what is the most likely underlying change?

choices.label: Thin, disconnected trabeculae with normal mineralisation (osteoporosis)
choices.feedback: Yes — reduced bone mass with normal mineral content.

choices.label: Unmineralised osteoid seams (osteomalacia)
choices.feedback: Possible in vitamin D deficiency, but the classic picture after menopause is osteoporosis; tests distinguish them.

s1.text: Which cell's activity has outpaced bone formation after menopause?

choices.label: Osteoclast
choices.feedback: Oestrogen loss increases osteoclast activity (via RANKL signalling), so resorption exceeds formation.

choices.label: Chondrocyte
choices.feedback: Chondrocytes are cartilage cells; they do not drive postmenopausal bone loss.

s2.text: What should happen after the fracture is treated?

choices.label: Refer for bone-density assessment and falls-risk review
choices.feedback: Right — secondary fracture prevention is a key step.

choices.label: Nothing more is needed once the cast is off
choices.feedback: A fragility fracture predicts future fractures; she needs evaluation.

end.text: Correct reasoning: osteoporosis (osteoclast > osteoblast activity) and secondary prevention by referral.

quiz.q: The central canal of an osteon is called the
quiz.why: Haversian canals run longitudinally; Volkmann's canals run across.
They form by fusion of monocyte-lineage precursors.

quiz.q: In osteoporosis the remaining bone is
options: normally mineralised but reduced in amount

quiz.q: Osteocytes communicate with each other through
quiz.why: Fine processes in canaliculi connect osteocytes via gap junctions.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — identify the slide from its description

scenes.text: Your viva partner reads out descriptions of slides.
Match each description to its organ.
Then tick your revision checklist.

steps.title: Organ clues that win spotters
steps.body:
- **Liver**: hexagonal lobules, central vein, portal triads (hepatic artery, portal vein, bile duct) at the corners.
- **Kidney**: glomeruli in the cortex with Bowman's capsule; tubules; medullary rays.
- **Thyroid**: follicles lined by cuboidal cells filled with pink colloid.
- **Lymph node**: capsule, subcapsular sinus, cortical follicles with germinal centres, medullary cords.
- **Spleen**: white pulp (lymphoid tissue around central arterioles) scattered in red pulp.
- **Pancreas**: serous acini with pale islets of Langerhans.
- **Skin (thick)**: thick keratin layer, no hair follicles — palm/sole.

steps.title: Exam technique
steps.body: State the tissue type first, then the identifying feature, then one clinical correlation. Example: 'Thyroid — follicles of cuboidal epithelium with colloid; in Graves' disease the epithelium becomes tall with scalloped colloid.'

courses.title: Embryology · From Fertilisation to the Heart
courses.summary: General embryology and development of the heart in words: gametogenesis, the first weeks, gastrulation, germ-layer derivatives, folding, and the common congenital heart defects with their embryological basis.
outcomes: Learners can sequence events of weeks 1–3 of development
Learners can list derivatives of ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm
Learners can explain septation of the heart and the basis of ASD, VSD and tetralogy of Fallot
Learners can describe the fetal circulation and changes at birth

lessons.title: Weeks 1–3: from zygote to trilaminar disc

scenes.text: A woman has a positive urine pregnancy test 2 weeks after a missed period.
By now the embryo is about 4 weeks after fertilisation.
What has the embryo already done? A lot.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Week 1
steps.body: Fertilisation usually occurs in the **ampulla** of the uterine tube. The zygote cleaves into a **morula** (about day 3–4), which becomes a **blastocyst** with an inner cell mass (embryoblast) and trophoblast. Implantation begins around **day 6–7**, usually in the posterior wall of the uterine body.

steps.title: Week 2 — the 'week of twos'
steps.body: Trophoblast forms cytotrophoblast and **syncytiotrophoblast** (which secretes hCG — the basis of pregnancy tests). The embryoblast forms a bilaminar disc of **epiblast** and **hypoblast**; two cavities appear (amniotic cavity and yolk sac).

steps.title: Week 3 — gastrulation
steps.body: The **primitive streak** appears on the epiblast. Epiblast cells migrate through it to form **endoderm** and **mesoderm**; remaining epiblast becomes **ectoderm**. The **notochord** forms and induces the overlying ectoderm to form the neural plate (neurulation begins).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying all three germ layers come from the hypoblast — they all come from the **epiblast**.
- Placing fertilisation in the uterus — it happens in the ampulla of the tube; implantation outside the uterus is an ectopic pregnancy.

activity.prompt: Put early development in order
items: Fertilisation in the ampulla
Morula
Blastocyst
Implantation begins
Bilaminar disc with hCG secretion
Primitive streak and gastrulation
Neural plate forms

quiz.q: The commonest site of fertilisation is the
quiz.why: The ampulla is the widest part of the tube.
Syncytiotrophoblast produces hCG that maintains the corpus luteum.

quiz.q: All three germ layers arise from the
quiz.why: Gastrulation converts epiblast into ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.
The primitive streak appears at the start of week 3.

scenes.text: Every organ belongs to one of three families: ectoderm, mesoderm, endoderm.
Knowing the family helps you predict which tissues a syndrome will affect.
Sort the tissues.

steps.title: Derivatives
steps.body:
- **Ectoderm**: epidermis, hair, nails, lens, enamel; **neuroectoderm** — brain, spinal cord, retina; **neural crest** — sensory and autonomic ganglia, Schwann cells, melanocytes, adrenal medulla, much of the face skeleton, conotruncal septum of the heart.
- **Mesoderm**: muscle (skeletal, cardiac, smooth), bone, cartilage, dermis, heart and vessels, blood, kidneys and gonads, adrenal cortex, spleen.
- **Endoderm**: epithelial lining of gut and respiratory tract, liver, pancreas, thyroid follicular cells, bladder epithelium (most), tonsillar and thymic epithelium.

steps.title: Shortcut
steps.body: Endoderm = the 'inner tubes' (lining of gut, airway and their glands). Mesoderm = what moves and carries (muscle, bone, blood, kidney). Ectoderm = surface and nervous system, with neural crest as the 'fourth germ layer'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Adrenal **medulla** is neural crest; adrenal **cortex** is mesoderm.
- The spleen is mesodermal, not endodermal, even though it sits with the gut.

It forms in the dorsal mesogastrium from mesenchyme.

quiz.why: The lung bud grows from the foregut endoderm.

lessons.title: Lab: Clinical case — a baby with a murmur

scenes.text: A 6-week-old has poor feeding and sweating during feeds.
You hear a harsh pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge.
Embryology explains what happened and why it matters.

steps.title: Heart septation in brief
steps.body:
- **Atria**: the septum primum grows down; ostium primum closes and ostium secundum opens in it; the septum secundum grows on its right side. The gap left in the septum secundum is the **foramen ovale**, with septum primum acting as its flap valve.
- **Ventricles**: a muscular septum grows up; the **membranous** part is completed by endocardial cushions and the conotruncal ridges. Most **VSDs** are in the membranous part.
- **Outflow**: neural-crest-derived conotruncal ridges spiral to form the aorticopulmonary septum. Unequal division with anterior displacement of the septum gives **tetralogy of Fallot**: pulmonary stenosis, overriding aorta, VSD, right ventricular hypertrophy.

steps.title: Fetal circulation
steps.body: Oxygenated blood from the placenta travels in the **umbilical vein**, bypasses much of the liver via the **ductus venosus**, crosses from right to left atrium through the **foramen ovale**, and pulmonary trunk blood passes to the aorta via the **ductus arteriosus**. At birth: lung expansion lowers pulmonary resistance, left atrial pressure rises and closes the foramen ovale; the ductus arteriosus constricts (prostaglandin levels fall, oxygen rises).

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: A baby with feeding difficulty, breathlessness, failure to thrive or cyanosis and a murmur needs prompt paediatric review and echocardiography.

s0.text: The 6-week-old sweats and tires during feeds. Pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge. Which lesion fits best?

choices.label: Ventricular septal defect
choices.feedback: Yes — a VSD typically gives a pansystolic murmur at the left lower sternal edge; symptoms appear as pulmonary resistance falls in the first weeks.

choices.label: Coarctation of the aorta
choices.feedback: Coarctation gives weak femoral pulses and a murmur at the back; the description fits VSD better.

s1.text: Where is the defect most likely located, embryologically?

choices.label: Membranous part of the interventricular septum
choices.feedback: Most VSDs are perimembranous, where endocardial cushions and conotruncal ridges must meet.

choices.label: Septum primum

s2.text: What is the right next step?

choices.label: Refer urgently to paediatric cardiology for echocardiography and heart failure management
choices.feedback: Correct — confirm, monitor growth, treat heart failure, and plan closure if needed.

choices.label: Tell the parents it is innocent and will vanish
choices.feedback: A symptomatic infant with a harsh murmur is not an innocent murmur.

end.text: Well reasoned: VSD from incomplete membranous septation; prompt referral is the right call.

quiz.q: Tetralogy of Fallot results mainly from
options: anterior displacement of the conotruncal (aorticopulmonary) septum
quiz.why: Unequal division of the outflow tract produces all four features.

quiz.q: The foramen ovale closes functionally at birth because
options: left atrial pressure rises above right atrial pressure
quiz.why: Increased pulmonary venous return raises left atrial pressure, pushing septum primum against septum secundum.

options: the umbilical vein to the IVC
the pulmonary trunk to the aorta
quiz.why: After birth it becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

quiz.why: Perimembranous VSDs are the commonest type.

story.title: The tour of the fetal heart

scenes.text: Imagine following a single red cell from the placenta.

steps.title: Remnants after birth
steps.body:
- Umbilical vein → **ligamentum teres hepatis**
- Ductus venosus → **ligamentum venosum**
- Foramen ovale → **fossa ovalis**
- Ductus arteriosus → **ligamentum arteriosum**
- Umbilical arteries (distal parts) → **medial umbilical ligaments**
- Allantois/urachus → **median umbilical ligament**

steps.title: Clinical link
steps.body: A patent ductus arteriosus gives a continuous 'machinery' murmur. In preterm babies it may close with drugs that inhibit prostaglandin synthesis; in some cyanotic heart diseases doctors keep it open with prostaglandin E1 until surgery.

courses.title: Neuroanatomy · Tracts, Cranial Nerves & Localisation
courses.summary: The spinal cord tracts, the brainstem and cranial nerves, and the blood supply of the brain — used to localise a lesion from the clinical signs, step by step.
outcomes: Learners can trace the corticospinal, dorsal column and spinothalamic pathways and where they cross
Learners can explain Brown-Séquard syndrome

lessons.title: The three long tracts and where they cross

scenes.text: A young man has a stab wound to the back at the mid-thoracic level.
His right leg is weak with poor vibration sense; his left leg cannot feel pinprick or temperature.
This odd pattern is a classic — once you know where the tracts cross.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: The pathways
steps.body:
- **Lateral corticospinal tract** (motor): cortex → internal capsule → cerebral peduncle → pyramid; **crosses at the pyramidal decussation in the lower medulla**; descends in the lateral column to anterior horn cells.
- **Dorsal column–medial lemniscus** (fine touch, vibration, proprioception): enters, ascends **ipsilaterally** in gracile/cuneate fasciculi, synapses in gracile/cuneate nuclei in the medulla, **crosses** as internal arcuate fibres, ascends as the medial lemniscus to the VPL thalamus.
- **Lateral spinothalamic tract** (pain, temperature): first-order neuron synapses in the dorsal horn; second-order fibres **cross within one or two segments** in the anterior white commissure and ascend contralaterally.

steps.title: Solved example · Brown-Séquard (right hemisection at T6)
steps.body:
Step 1: corticospinal fibres have already crossed → **right** leg weak (UMN signs below the lesion).
Step 2: dorsal columns ascend uncrossed → **right** loss of vibration/proprioception below the lesion.
Step 3: spinothalamic fibres crossed below → **left** loss of pain and temperature starting about one to two segments below the level.

So: same-side motor and dorsal-column loss, opposite-side pain/temperature loss.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the dorsal columns cross in the spinal cord — they cross in the **medulla**.
- Forgetting the 1–2 segment offset for spinothalamic loss.

lessons.title: Lab: UMN or LMN? Sort the signs

scenes.text: Two patients: one with a stroke, one with a nerve injury.
Both are weak, but the signs differ.
Sort the signs.

steps.title: UMN vs LMN
steps.body:
**Upper motor neuron** (cortex to anterior horn): spasticity (clasp-knife), brisk reflexes, extensor plantar (Babinski), little wasting, weakness in a pyramidal pattern.

**Lower motor neuron** (anterior horn cell, root, nerve): flaccidity, reduced or absent reflexes, marked wasting, fasciculations, flexor or absent plantar.

steps.title: Facial palsy — the classic test
steps.body:
The part of the facial motor nucleus supplying the **forehead** receives cortical input from **both** hemispheres; the lower face receives mainly contralateral input. So:
- **UMN lesion** (stroke): weakness of the **lower face** on the opposite side, forehead spared.
- **LMN lesion** (Bell's palsy, facial nerve): the **whole half of the face** on the same side, including the forehead.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying spinal shock gives brisk reflexes from day one — acutely after cord injury reflexes may be absent.
- Calling forehead-sparing facial weakness 'Bell's palsy' — forehead sparing suggests a central (UMN) cause.

lessons.title: Lab: Clinical case — sudden weakness and the arteries

scenes.text: A 64-year-old woman suddenly cannot move her right arm and leg and cannot find her words.
Her family brings her within an hour.
Which artery? And what must happen fast?

steps.title: Arterial territories
steps.body:
- **Middle cerebral artery (MCA)**: lateral surface — face and arm area of motor/sensory cortex; Broca's and Wernicke's areas in the dominant (usually left) hemisphere. Contralateral face/arm > leg weakness, aphasia (dominant) or neglect (non-dominant). Its lenticulostriate branches supply the internal capsule.
- **Anterior cerebral artery (ACA)**: medial surface — leg area. Contralateral **leg** > arm weakness.
- **Posterior cerebral artery (PCA)**: occipital lobe — contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
- **Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome**: PICA/vertebral — ipsilateral face pain/temperature loss, contralateral body pain/temperature loss, ataxia, dysphagia, Horner's.

steps.title: Time is brain
steps.body: Suspected stroke is an emergency: call **112**, note the time last seen well, and get to a stroke-ready hospital. Clot-dissolving or clot-retrieval treatments work only within time windows and need a brain scan first to exclude bleeding.

steps.title: Key cranial nerve facts
steps.body:
- Midbrain: **III** (eye down and out, ptosis, dilated pupil if compressive), **IV** (superior oblique — trouble looking down and in, e.g. reading or stairs).
- Pons: **V** (sensation of face, muscles of mastication), **VI** (lateral rectus — cannot abduct), **VII** (facial expression, taste anterior two-thirds), **VIII**.
- Medulla: **IX, X** (palate, gag, voice), **XI** (sternocleidomastoid, trapezius), **XII** (tongue deviates **towards** the side of an LMN lesion).

A painful third-nerve palsy with a dilated pupil may be a posterior communicating artery aneurysm — an emergency.

steps.title: Rule of 4 (memory aid)
steps.body: Four cranial nerve nuclei groups in the medulla (IX–XII), four in the pons (V–VIII), two in the midbrain (III–IV). The motor nuclei of III, IV, VI and XII lie near the midline — so medial brainstem lesions affect them along with the corticospinal tract.

courses.title: Enzymes · Kinetics, Inhibition & Clinical Enzymology
courses.summary: How enzymes work, Michaelis–Menten kinetics, types of inhibition (with drug examples) and enzymes used as diagnostic markers.
outcomes: Learners can apply the Michaelis–Menten equation and interpret Km and Vmax
Learners can distinguish competitive, non-competitive and irreversible inhibition
Learners can name clinically important enzyme markers
Learners can reason through an enzyme-based clinical case

lessons.title: How enzymes work and Michaelis–Menten kinetics

scenes.text: In the lab, adding more substrate speeds a reaction — until it suddenly stops speeding up.
The curve flattens like a hyperbola.
That plateau is Vmax.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Key ideas
steps.body:
Enzymes lower **activation energy**; they do not change ΔG or equilibrium. The Michaelis–Menten equation: **v = Vmax [S] ÷ (Km + [S])**.

- **Km** = substrate concentration at half Vmax; a **low Km means high affinity**.
- **Vmax** depends on enzyme amount.
- Lineweaver–Burk (double reciprocal) plot: y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = −1/Km.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Vmax = 100 µmol/min, Km = 2 mM.
- [S] = 2 mM: v = 100 × 2 ÷ 4 = **50** (half Vmax, as expected).
- [S] = 6 mM: v = 100 × 6 ÷ 8 = **75 µmol/min**.
- [S] = 18 mM (9 × Km): v = 100 × 18 ÷ 20 = **90** — you need [S] = 9 Km to reach 90% of Vmax.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying enzymes shift equilibrium — they only speed up reaching it.
- Reading a high Km as high affinity — it is the opposite.

lessons.title: Lab: Inhibition numericals and drug examples

scenes.text: A man drinks illicit liquor and develops blurred vision.
Doctors give fomepizole or ethanol to block an enzyme.
This is competitive inhibition in action.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Competitive**: inhibitor resembles substrate and binds the active site. **Km ↑, Vmax unchanged**; overcome by more substrate. Examples: methotrexate (dihydrofolate reductase), statins (HMG-CoA reductase), ethanol/fomepizole vs methanol at alcohol dehydrogenase.
- **Non-competitive**: binds elsewhere; **Vmax ↓, Km unchanged**.
- **Irreversible**: covalent modification — aspirin acetylates COX; organophosphates phosphorylate acetylcholinesterase.

steps.title: Solved example · Competitive inhibition
steps.body:
Apparent Km = Km × (1 + [I]/Ki). Km 2 mM, [I] 4 µM, Ki 2 µM → Km(app) = 2 × 3 = **6 mM**.
With Vmax 100 and [S] 6 mM: v = 100 × 6 ÷ (6 + 6) = **50** (versus 75 without inhibitor).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying competitive inhibitors reduce Vmax — they don't; enough substrate wins.
- Treating aspirin as reversible — its effect on platelets lasts the platelet's lifetime.

steps.title: Diagnostic enzymes and markers
steps.body:
- **Cardiac troponin (I or T)** — the preferred marker of myocardial injury; rises within hours and stays raised for days. (Troponin is a structural protein, not an enzyme, but is taught with cardiac markers.)
- **CK-MB** — rises and falls faster; useful for reinfarction.
- **ALT** (liver-specific), **AST** (liver, heart, muscle) — AST:ALT > 2 suggests alcoholic liver disease.
- **ALP and GGT** — cholestasis; ALP also bone.
- **Amylase and lipase** — acute pancreatitis (lipase more specific).
- **LDH** — tissue damage, haemolysis, tumour burden.

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: Chest pain with ECG changes is managed by protocol immediately — do not wait for a blood result to call the senior or start treatment.

scenes.text: A sprinter's muscles make lactate; a marathoner burns glucose fully to CO₂.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Glycolysis
steps.body: Cytosol; glucose → 2 pyruvate. Irreversible regulated steps: **hexokinase/glucokinase**, **phosphofructokinase-1** (rate-limiting; activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate, inhibited by ATP and citrate), **pyruvate kinase**. Net: **2 ATP + 2 NADH** per glucose. Anaerobically, lactate dehydrogenase regenerates NAD⁺ (red cells always do this — no mitochondria).

steps.title: Aerobic fate
steps.body: Pyruvate dehydrogenase (needs thiamine, lipoate, CoA, FAD, NAD⁺) → acetyl-CoA → TCA cycle in mitochondria → NADH and FADH₂ → electron transport chain. Using modern P/O ratios (2.5 per NADH, 1.5 per FADH₂), total ≈ **30–32 ATP per glucose** (older textbooks say 36–38).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting red cells rely on glycolysis only.
- Quoting 38 ATP without noting it is an older theoretical value.

scenes.text: A 20-year-old man is given an antimalarial (primaquine) and develops jaundice and dark urine.
His brother had similar trouble after eating fava beans.
It is the HMP shunt.

steps.title: HMP shunt (pentose phosphate pathway)
steps.body: Oxidative phase: **glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase** (rate-limiting) produces **NADPH**; non-oxidative phase makes ribose-5-phosphate. NADPH keeps glutathione reduced, protecting red cells from oxidants. In **G6PD deficiency** (X-linked, common in India, Africa and the Mediterranean), oxidant stress (primaquine, dapsone, some sulfonamides, fava beans, infections) causes acute haemolysis. Blood film: **Heinz bodies** and bite cells.

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: Acute haemolysis with dark urine needs urgent medical review: stop the trigger, check haemoglobin and renal function. Doctors screen for G6PD before giving primaquine for radical cure of vivax malaria.

steps.title: Glycogen metabolism
steps.body:
Synthesis: **glycogen synthase** (insulin activates). Breakdown: **glycogen phosphorylase** (glucagon in liver, adrenaline in muscle) and debranching enzyme. Liver uses **glucose-6-phosphatase** to release free glucose; muscle lacks it, so muscle glycogen fuels the muscle only.

- **Von Gierke (type I)**: glucose-6-phosphatase — severe fasting hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, lactic acidosis, hyperuricaemia, hyperlipidaemia.
- **Pompe (type II)**: lysosomal acid α-glucosidase — cardiomegaly, hypotonia in infants.
- **Cori (type III)**: debranching enzyme — milder hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly.
- **McArdle (type V)**: muscle phosphorylase — exercise cramps, myoglobinuria, no rise in lactate on exercise.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Expecting hypoglycaemia in McArdle disease — the liver is normal.
- Forgetting Pompe is lysosomal and affects the heart.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — gluconeogenesis and the fasting patient

steps.title: Gluconeogenesis
steps.body:
Makes glucose from **lactate, alanine (and other glucogenic amino acids), glycerol** in the liver (and kidney). Bypass enzymes: **pyruvate carboxylase** (biotin; activated by acetyl-CoA), **PEPCK**, **fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase**, **glucose-6-phosphatase**. Even-chain fatty acids cannot give net glucose (acetyl-CoA cannot become pyruvate).

Fasting sequence: hepatic glycogen supports glucose for about the first day; gluconeogenesis rises; with prolonged fasting ketone bodies increasingly fuel the brain, sparing protein.

steps.title: Alcohol and hypoglycaemia
steps.body: Ethanol metabolism raises NADH, which pushes pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, blocking gluconeogenesis — so heavy drinking while fasting can cause dangerous hypoglycaemia.

steps.title: β-oxidation
steps.body: Long-chain fatty acids are activated to acyl-CoA, then carried into mitochondria by the **carnitine shuttle** (CPT-I is rate-limiting; inhibited by **malonyl-CoA**, so synthesis and oxidation don't run together). Each cycle shortens the chain by 2 carbons, yielding acetyl-CoA, NADH and FADH₂.

steps.title: Ketogenesis
steps.body: In liver mitochondria (key enzyme **HMG-CoA synthase**), acetyl-CoA → acetoacetate → β-hydroxybutyrate (and acetone). The liver cannot use ketones (lacks thiophorase / succinyl-CoA:acetoacetate CoA transferase); brain, heart and muscle can. Excess production in insulin deficiency → DKA.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying the liver uses its own ketones.
- Forgetting that urine dipsticks (nitroprusside) detect acetoacetate, not β-hydroxybutyrate.

scenes.text: A patient's report lists total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides.
Each lipoprotein is a delivery truck with a route.
Sort their features.

steps.title: Lipoproteins
steps.body:
- **Chylomicrons** (apo B-48, C-II, E): dietary TG from gut to tissues.
- **VLDL** (apo B-100): liver TG to tissues → IDL → LDL.
- **LDL** (apo B-100): cholesterol to tissues; taken up by **LDL receptor**; 'bad' — drives atherosclerosis.
- **HDL** (apo A-I): reverse cholesterol transport to the liver; LCAT esterifies cholesterol.

**Lipoprotein lipase** (activated by apo C-II) hydrolyses TG in chylomicrons and VLDL.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying apo B-48 is on LDL — B-48 is only on chylomicrons.
- Thinking HDL carries cholesterol *to* tissues.

steps.title: Familial hypercholesterolaemia (FH)
steps.body: Usually an autosomal dominant defect in the **LDL receptor** (also apo B or PCSK9 gene variants). LDL cannot be cleared → very high LDL from birth, tendon xanthomas, corneal arcus at a young age, premature coronary disease. Homozygotes are severely affected in childhood.

steps.title: Treatment principles
steps.body: Lifestyle plus **statins** (inhibit HMG-CoA reductase → liver cells make more LDL receptors), ezetimibe (blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption via NPC1L1), PCSK9 inhibitors. **Cascade screening** of relatives finds others at risk.

steps.title: When to see a professional
steps.body: Anyone with a family history of heart attack before about 55 (men) or 65 (women) should ask a doctor about lipid testing.

steps.title: Learning note

steps.title: B-complex and C
steps.body:
- **B1 thiamine** (TPP): PDH, α-KG dehydrogenase, transketolase → beriberi (dry: neuropathy; wet: heart failure), **Wernicke–Korsakoff** in alcohol use.
- **B2 riboflavin** (FAD/FMN): angular stomatitis, cheilosis, glossitis.
- **B3 niacin** (NAD/NADP): **pellagra** — dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia (and death); also in Hartnup disease and carcinoid.
- **B6 pyridoxine** (PLP): transamination, haem synthesis; isoniazid causes deficiency → neuropathy, sideroblastic anaemia.
- **B7 biotin**: carboxylases.
- **B9 folate** and **B12**: one-carbon metabolism, DNA synthesis → megaloblastic anaemia.
- **C ascorbate**: hydroxylation of proline/lysine in collagen → **scurvy** (bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages, poor wound healing).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving glucose before thiamine to a malnourished alcohol-dependent patient — it can precipitate Wernicke's; thiamine is given first or with it.
- Mixing pellagra (niacin) with scurvy (vitamin C).

scenes.text: A 55-year-old vegetarian is pale, tired and has tingling feet and unsteady walking in the dark.
Blood shows macrocytic anaemia.
Folate or B12? It matters.

steps.title: B12 and folate
steps.body:
Both are needed for thymidine (DNA) synthesis → deficiency gives **megaloblastic anaemia** with hypersegmented neutrophils. **B12 only**: methylmalonyl-CoA mutase (raised methylmalonic acid) and neurological damage — **subacute combined degeneration** of dorsal and lateral columns. Causes of B12 deficiency: strict vegetarian diet, **pernicious anaemia** (antibodies to intrinsic factor/parietal cells), ileal disease or resection, metformin (long-term).

Giving folate alone to a B12-deficient patient can improve the blood picture while nerve damage progresses.

steps.title: When to see a professional
steps.body: Neurological symptoms with anaemia need prompt medical assessment; treatment is supervised and often by injection.

steps.title: A, D, E, K
steps.body:
- **A**: rhodopsin (vision), epithelial health → night blindness, xerophthalmia, Bitot's spots, keratomalacia; excess is toxic and teratogenic.
- **D**: calcitriol raises Ca²⁺/phosphate absorption → **rickets** (children), **osteomalacia** (adults).
- **E**: antioxidant → haemolysis, neuropathy (rare).
- **K**: γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, X (and proteins C, S) → bleeding; newborns get prophylactic vitamin K at birth. Warfarin antagonises vitamin K recycling.

steps.title: Kwashiorkor vs marasmus
steps.body:
**Marasmus**: severe deficiency of energy and protein — severe wasting ('skin and bones'), no oedema, alert but hungry.
**Kwashiorkor**: oedema (low albumin among other mechanisms), fatty liver, 'flaky paint' skin, hair changes, apathy; weight may be less reduced because of oedema.

Children with **bilateral pitting oedema** or severe wasting have severe acute malnutrition and need referral for structured treatment (stabilisation then rehabilitation).

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: Severe acute malnutrition with complications (poor appetite, infection, hypothermia, hypoglycaemia) is an emergency: refer to a facility with a nutrition rehabilitation unit.

scenes.text: A block of 10,000 adults is surveyed: 800 already have diabetes.
Over the next year, 46 new cases appear among those without diabetes.
Which number is incidence and which is prevalence?

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Ratio**: one quantity divided by another (e.g. sex ratio). **Proportion**: numerator included in denominator (often %). **Rate**: proportion with a time element.
- **Incidence (rate)** = new cases during a period ÷ population **at risk** during that period. Measures risk; used for causation studies.
- **Point prevalence** = all existing cases at a point in time ÷ total population. Measures burden; used for planning services.
- **Relationship** (stable conditions): **Prevalence ≈ Incidence × mean Duration**.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Prevalence = 800 ÷ 10,000 = **8%**.
Incidence: population at risk = 10,000 − 800 = 9,200. Incidence = 46 ÷ 9,200 = 0.005 = **5 per 1,000 per year**.

If incidence is 5 per 1,000/year and average duration of a disease is 4 years, prevalence ≈ 5 × 4 = **20 per 1,000**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the whole population (including existing cases) as the denominator for incidence.
- Thinking a new treatment that prolongs life lowers prevalence — longer survival **raises** prevalence.

lessons.title: Lab: Outbreak numericals — attack and fatality rates

scenes.text: After a wedding feast, 240 of 600 guests develop vomiting and diarrhoea.
12 of the ill guests need admission; 2 die.
Calculate the rates the district surveillance officer needs.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Attack and case fatality rates
steps.body:
Attack rate = cases ÷ population exposed × 100 = 240 ÷ 600 = **40%**.
Case fatality rate = deaths ÷ cases × 100 = 2 ÷ 240 = **0.83%**.

CFR measures the **killing power** of a disease among those affected, not the risk in the population.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Secondary attack rate
steps.body:
SAR = (new cases among contacts within the incubation period) ÷ (susceptible contacts) × 100.
A measles case has 30 susceptible household/school contacts; 6 fall ill within one incubation period → SAR = 6 ÷ 30 = **20%**. The primary case is excluded from numerator and denominator.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the total population instead of the exposed population for attack rate.
- Counting the primary case in SAR.

scenes.text: The District Health Officer must present infant and maternal mortality.
Data: 10,000 live births, 300 infant deaths, 15 maternal deaths.
Calculate the indicators.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
- **Infant mortality rate (IMR)** = deaths under 1 year ÷ live births in the same year × 1,000.
- **Neonatal mortality rate** = deaths in the first 28 days ÷ live births × 1,000.
- **Under-5 mortality rate** — per 1,000 live births.
- **Maternal mortality ratio (MMR)** = maternal deaths ÷ live births × **100,000**.
- **Crude birth/death rate** — per 1,000 mid-year population.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
IMR = 300 ÷ 10,000 × 1,000 = **30 per 1,000 live births**.
MMR = 15 ÷ 10,000 × 100,000 = **150 per 100,000 live births**.

IMR is considered one of the most sensitive indicators of a population's health and socio-economic status.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using total population as denominator for IMR — the denominator is **live births**.
- Expressing MMR per 1,000 — it is per **100,000** live births.

steps.title: Outbreak investigation steps
steps.body:
1. Confirm the diagnosis (clinical + lab). 2. Confirm the outbreak (compare with expected numbers). 3. Define a case and search for cases. 4. Describe by **time, place, person** (epidemic curve, spot map). 5. Form hypotheses. 6. Test them (analytical study). 7. Implement control measures (often early, in parallel). 8. Communicate findings and keep surveillance going.

In India, disease surveillance is coordinated through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP/IHIP) — report outbreaks per its guidance.

steps.title: Epidemic curve
steps.body: A point-source outbreak shows a single sharp peak within one incubation period; a propagated (person-to-person) outbreak shows successive, wider waves.

scenes.text: A company offers a rapid test for a disease. It is tried on 1,000 people; 100 truly have the disease.
The test is positive in 90 of the diseased and 45 of the healthy.
How good is it?

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
|  | Disease + | Disease − |
- Test + : **a** = true positives (TP), **b** = false positives (FP)
- Test − : **c** = false negatives (FN), **d** = true negatives (TN)

- **Sensitivity** = a ÷ (a + c) — ability to detect the diseased (true positive rate).
- **Specificity** = d ÷ (b + d) — ability to identify the healthy (true negative rate).
- **PPV** = a ÷ (a + b) — probability of disease if positive.
- **NPV** = d ÷ (c + d) — probability of no disease if negative.

steps.title: Memory aids
steps.body: **SnNout**: a highly **S**ensitive test, when **N**egative, rules **out**. **SpPin**: a highly **Sp**ecific test, when **P**ositive, rules **in**.

activity.prompt: A test has TP 80, FN 20, FP 90, TN 810. What is its PPV in %? (one decimal)

scenes.text: The same test (sensitivity 90%, specificity 95%) is used in a specialist hospital (prevalence 50%) and a general population camp (prevalence 1%).
Is a positive result equally trustworthy in both?
Calculate.

steps.title: Solved example · 10,000 people each
steps.body:
**Hospital (prevalence 50%)**: diseased 5,000 → TP 4,500, FN 500; healthy 5,000 → FP 250, TN 4,750. PPV = 4,500 ÷ 4,750 = **94.7%**.

**Camp (prevalence 1%)**: diseased 100 → TP 90, FN 10; healthy 9,900 → FP 495, TN 9,405. PPV = 90 ÷ 585 = **15.4%**.

Same sensitivity and specificity, but at low prevalence most positives are **false positives**.

steps.title: Likelihood ratios
steps.body: LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity); LR− = (1 − sensitivity) ÷ specificity. For our test: LR+ = 0.90 ÷ 0.05 = **18**; LR− = 0.10 ÷ 0.95 ≈ **0.11**. LRs do not depend on prevalence and help update a pre-test probability.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking sensitivity/specificity change with prevalence — predictive values do; sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test (in a given population spectrum).
- Screening very low-prevalence groups without planning for confirmatory tests.

lessons.title: Lab: Series and parallel testing — sort the strategies

scenes.text: National HIV testing uses several different rapid tests in sequence.
Why test in series? Why sometimes in parallel?
Sort the properties.

steps.title: Combining tests
steps.body:
- **Series (sequential)**: positive only if **all** tests are positive → **specificity ↑**, sensitivity ↓. Used to confirm a diagnosis (e.g. confirmatory HIV algorithm) and to reduce false positives.
- **Parallel (simultaneous)**: positive if **any** test is positive → **sensitivity ↑**, specificity ↓. Used when missing a case is dangerous (emergency rule-outs).

Choosing a cut-off: lowering the threshold raises sensitivity and lowers specificity (and vice versa) — shown by the ROC curve.

steps.title: Exam angle
steps.body: Blood bank screening prioritises sensitivity (don't miss infected donations); confirming a diagnosis before labelling a person prioritises specificity.

steps.title: Criteria for a screening programme (Wilson–Jungner, adapted)
steps.body:
- The condition is an important health problem.
- Its natural history is understood, with a recognisable latent/early stage.
- An acceptable, valid and reliable test exists.
- Effective, accepted treatment for early disease exists, and early treatment improves outcomes.
- Facilities for diagnosis and treatment are available.
- Agreed policy on whom to treat; costs balanced against benefits; screening is a continuing process.

India's population-based screening for common non-communicable diseases (hypertension, diabetes, common cancers) for adults aged 30 and above is delivered through primary health care.

steps.title: Biases
steps.body: **Lead-time bias** (earlier diagnosis makes survival look longer without real benefit), **length bias** (screening picks up slow-growing disease), **overdiagnosis**.

scenes.text: Researchers want to know whether smoking causes lung cancer.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Hierarchy
steps.body:
- **Descriptive**: case report/series, cross-sectional (prevalence surveys) — generate hypotheses.
- **Ecological**: groups, not individuals (risk of ecological fallacy).
- **Case-control**: start with cases and controls, look back at exposure → **odds ratio**; good for rare diseases; prone to recall bias.
- **Cohort**: start with exposed and unexposed, follow forward → **incidence, relative risk, attributable risk**; good for rare exposures; costly, loss to follow-up.
- **Randomised controlled trial (RCT)**: randomisation balances known and unknown confounders; blinding reduces bias; gold standard for interventions.
- **Systematic review/meta-analysis**: pools evidence.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calculating relative risk from a case-control study — use the odds ratio.
- Calling a cross-sectional study 'longitudinal'.

lessons.title: Lab: Relative risk, odds ratio and attributable risk

scenes.text: A cohort follows 1,000 tobacco chewers and 1,000 non-chewers for 10 years.
30 chewers and 10 non-chewers develop oral cancer.
Calculate the measures of association.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Cohort
steps.body:
Incidence in exposed = 30 ÷ 1,000 = 0.030; unexposed = 10 ÷ 1,000 = 0.010.
- **RR** = 0.030 ÷ 0.010 = **3** (chewers have 3 times the risk).
- **Attributable risk (risk difference)** = 0.030 − 0.010 = **0.020** = 20 per 1,000.
- **Attributable risk %** (in exposed) = 0.020 ÷ 0.030 = **66.7%** of cancers in chewers are due to chewing (if causal).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Case-control
steps.body:
Cases 100 (40 exposed, 60 not); controls 100 (20 exposed, 80 not).
OR = (a × d) ÷ (b × c) = (40 × 80) ÷ (60 × 20) = 3,200 ÷ 1,200 = **2.67**. For a rare disease the OR approximates the RR.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Placing cells in the wrong order — keep a = exposed cases, b = exposed non-cases (or controls), c = unexposed cases, d = unexposed non-cases.
- Reading RR = 1 as 'protective' — RR = 1 means no association; RR < 1 suggests protection.

scenes.text: In a 5-year trial, 20% of controls and 15% of treated patients had a heart attack.
The press release says 'risk cut by 25%!'
How many patients must be treated to prevent one heart attack?

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Control event rate (CER) = 0.20; experimental event rate (EER) = 0.15.
- **ARR** = CER − EER = **0.05** (5 percentage points).
- **RRR** = ARR ÷ CER = 0.05 ÷ 0.20 = **25%** — the press-release number.
- **NNT** = 1 ÷ ARR = 1 ÷ 0.05 = **20** — treat 20 people for 5 years to prevent one heart attack.

Number needed to harm (NNH) = 1 ÷ absolute risk increase of an adverse effect.

steps.title: Reading claims
steps.body: Relative risk reductions sound large; always ask for the absolute risk reduction and NNT, and over what time period.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using percentages directly (1 ÷ 5 = 0.2) — convert 5% to 0.05 first.
- Forgetting to round NNT **up** to a whole number.

steps.title: Bias and confounding
steps.body:
- **Selection bias**: groups differ in how they were selected (e.g. hospital controls, volunteers, loss to follow-up).
- **Information/measurement bias**: recall bias, interviewer bias, misclassification.
- **Confounding**: a third factor associated with both exposure and outcome, not on the causal pathway (e.g. smoking confounds the link between coffee and lung cancer). Controlled by randomisation, restriction, matching, stratification and multivariable analysis.
- **Hawthorne effect**: people change behaviour because they know they're observed.

steps.title: Causation
steps.body: Bradford Hill considerations: strength, consistency, specificity, temporality (exposure before outcome — essential), biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy.

lessons.title: Levels of prevention and health care delivery

scenes.text: On a Village Health and Nutrition Day, the ASHA, ANM and anganwadi worker meet mothers and elders.
Each activity sits at a different level of prevention.
Name them.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Levels of prevention
steps.body:
- **Primordial**: prevent emergence of risk factors (healthy lifestyles from childhood, tobacco control policies).
- **Primary**: prevent disease onset — health promotion and specific protection (immunisation, iodised salt, bed nets).
- **Secondary**: early diagnosis and prompt treatment (screening, case finding).
- **Tertiary**: limit disability and rehabilitate (physiotherapy after stroke, prosthetics).

steps.title: Structure (general)
steps.body: Village level: **ASHA** (community health activist) and anganwadi worker; **Sub-centre / Ayushman Arogya Mandir (Health & Wellness Centre)** with ANM/community health officer; **Primary Health Centre (PHC)** with a medical officer; **Community Health Centre (CHC)** as first referral unit; then sub-district and district hospitals, and tertiary medical colleges. The **National Health Mission** supports this system; Ayushman Bharat includes health and wellness centres and a health insurance scheme (PM-JAY). Population norms vary for plains and hilly/tribal areas.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling screening 'primary prevention' — it is secondary.
- Treating rehabilitation as unimportant — tertiary prevention restores function.

lessons.title: Lab: Sort the national programme aims (general terms)

scenes.text: As a PHC medical officer you will implement several national programmes.

steps.title: Programmes in general terms
steps.body:
- **National TB Elimination Programme**: case finding, rapid molecular testing, free treatment with adherence support, nutritional support, notification.
- **Vector-borne disease control** (malaria, dengue, kala-azar, filariasis, JE, chikungunya): surveillance, diagnosis and treatment, vector control, mass drug administration for filariasis.
- **Universal Immunisation Programme**: free vaccines for children and pregnant women per the national schedule.
- **Reproductive, maternal, newborn, child and adolescent health (RMNCH+A)**: antenatal care, institutional delivery, newborn care, family planning, adolescent health.
- **NCD programme**: population-based screening for hypertension, diabetes and common cancers (oral, breast, cervical) from age 30, lifestyle counselling.
- **National Leprosy Eradication Programme**, **National AIDS Control Programme**, **National Mental Health Programme / Tele-MANAS**.

Details (schedules, targets, drug regimens) change — always use the current official guidelines.

steps.title: Your role
steps.body: Implement, record and report accurately; supervise field staff; involve the community.

lessons.title: Lab: Cold chain and safe immunisation

scenes.text: An ANM arrives at a session site with a vaccine carrier.
A vial monitor has changed colour on one vial.
What should she do?

steps.title: Cold chain
steps.body: Vaccines are stored and transported in a chain of equipment (walk-in coolers, ice-lined refrigerators, deep freezers, vaccine carriers with conditioned ice packs). Most routine vaccines are kept at **+2 to +8 °C**. **Freeze-sensitive** vaccines (e.g. hepatitis B, pentavalent, TT/Td, IPV) must not be frozen — the **shake test** checks suspected freezing. **Heat-sensitive** vaccines include OPV and measles–rubella. **Vaccine vial monitors (VVMs)**: if the inner square matches or is darker than the outer circle, discard.

steps.title: Safe immunisation
steps.body: Auto-disable syringes, no recapping, hub cutters/sharps containers, correct site and route, observe for **30 minutes** after vaccination for adverse events, and report **AEFI** (adverse events following immunisation) per guidelines. Reconstituted measles–rubella vaccine is used within the recommended time and kept cold.

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: Any serious AEFI (anaphylaxis, seizure, death, hospitalisation) needs immediate care and reporting.
