steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Primary lesions
steps.body:
- **Macule** (flat, < 1 cm) / **patch** (flat, ≥ 1 cm).
- **Papule** (raised, < 1 cm) / **plaque** (raised, ≥ 1 cm, flat-topped).
- **Nodule** (deep, ≥ 1 cm).
- **Vesicle** (fluid, < 1 cm) / **bulla** (≥ 1 cm).
- **Pustule** (pus), **wheal** (transient oedema).

steps.title: Secondary & description
steps.body: Scale, crust, erosion, ulcer, lichenification, excoriation. Then: distribution (flexural, extensor, dermatomal, photo-exposed), arrangement (annular, linear, grouped), colour, border, number, symmetry. Always check nails, hair, mucosa.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling everything a 'rash'; forgetting to examine mucous membranes; not using good light.

scenes.text: A child with flexural itchy patches, a man with silvery plaques on elbows, a student with an expanding ring in the groin.
Patterns tell them apart.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body:
- **Atopic eczema:** itchy, ill-defined, flexural in older children, dry skin, atopy history.
- **Psoriasis:** well-defined red plaques with silvery scale, extensor surfaces, scalp, nails (pitting, onycholysis); associated arthritis.
- **Tinea (dermatophyte):** annular with active scaly edge and central clearing, itchy; KOH microscopy confirms.

steps.title: Steroid misuse epidemic
steps.body: Over-the-counter topical steroid (often combination creams) misuse on tinea in India has produced widespread chronic, extensive and treatment-resistant dermatophytosis ('tinea incognito'). Avoid steroid–antifungal combinations; treat with appropriate antifungals per current guidance and counsel adherence and hygiene.

steps.title: Eczema care
steps.body: Emollients generously, avoid irritants (soap), topical steroids of appropriate potency for flares with correct quantity and duration.

steps.title: Acne
steps.body: Comedones (open/closed), papules, pustules, nodules/cysts, scars. Treatment ladder: topical retinoid and benzoyl peroxide, topical/oral antibiotics in combination (not alone, to limit resistance), hormonal options in women, isotretinoin by specialists for severe/scarring acne (teratogenic — strict pregnancy prevention, mood monitoring).

steps.title: Psychological impact
steps.body: Acne can cause significant distress; screen for low mood. If thoughts of self-harm, provide support and help (Tele-MANAS 14416, emergency 112).

steps.title: Myths
steps.body: Acne isn't caused by dirt; aggressive scrubbing worsens it. Diet links are modest; avoid blame.

A burrow is pathognomonic.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Recognise
steps.body: Intense nocturnal itch, papules and burrows in finger webs, wrists, axillae, waist, genitalia; family/close contacts itching. Infants may have palms/soles involvement.

steps.title: Treat
steps.body: Topical scabicide (e.g., permethrin) applied from neck down (include scalp/face in infants per guidance) and repeated per protocol; **treat all close contacts simultaneously**; wash bedding/clothes in hot water or seal in a bag; itch may persist 2–4 weeks after successful treatment. Oral ivermectin in selected cases per guidance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Treating only the patient; using topical steroids alone; not explaining post-scabetic itch.

lessons.title: Lab: Leprosy — don't miss the patch

scenes.text: A 35-year-old farmer has a pale patch on his forearm that he can't feel; he burnt his hand without noticing.
India still reports many of the world's new leprosy cases.

steps.title: Cardinal signs (WHO)
steps.body:
1. Definite loss of sensation in a pale (hypopigmented) or reddish skin patch.
2. Thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensation and/or weakness of muscles supplied.
3. Acid-fast bacilli in a slit-skin smear.
One cardinal sign is enough for diagnosis.

steps.title: Classify and treat
steps.body: Paucibacillary (1–5 lesions, no bacilli) vs multibacillary (> 5 lesions, nerve involvement, or positive smear) guides multidrug therapy (MDT) duration under the national programme, free of cost. Watch for reactions (type 1, type 2/ENL) and nerve damage; prevent disability with self-care.

steps.title: Stigma
steps.body: Leprosy is curable; patients on MDT quickly become non-infectious. Use respectful language; avoid outdated terms.

lessons.title: Lab: Case — fever, blistering and mucosal erosions

scenes.text: A 40-year-old started an anticonvulsant 3 weeks ago. Now fever, painful dusky skin, blisters, erosions in mouth and eyes.
A skin emergency.

steps.title: SJS/TEN
steps.body: Severe mucocutaneous reaction, usually drug-induced (e.g., some anticonvulsants, allopurinol, sulfonamides, nevirapine, NSAIDs of certain classes), typically 4–28 days after starting. Prodromal fever, painful skin, target-like dusky lesions, blisters, positive Nikolsky sign, mucosal involvement (≥ 2 sites). SJS < 10% BSA detachment; TEN > 30%; overlap between.

steps.title: Act
steps.body: **Stop the culprit drug immediately**, admit (burns unit/ICU for extensive disease), fluids, wound care, eye care (ophthalmology early), nutrition, pain control, infection surveillance; specialist-led therapy. Document allergy clearly.

steps.title: DRESS
steps.body: Fever, widespread rash, facial swelling, lymphadenopathy, eosinophilia, organ involvement (liver), 2–8 weeks after drug start — also stop drug and escalate.

s1.text: Fever, painful dusky skin, blisters, oral and ocular erosions, started an anticonvulsant 3 weeks ago.

choices.label: TEN — manage in ICU/burns unit with fluids, wound and eye care

end.text: The patient is cared for in the burns unit; a drug-allergy alert is recorded and the family counselled.

scenes.text: Two patients with red swollen legs: one with gradual spread and fever, one with pain out of proportion, rapidly spreading, and hypotension.

steps.title: Cellulitis
steps.body: Spreading erythema, warmth, tenderness, swelling ± fever; look for entry (tinea pedis, wounds). Mark margins, oral/IV antibiotics per severity guidance, elevate, treat entry point.

steps.title: Necrotising fasciitis
steps.body: Pain out of proportion to signs, rapid progression, systemic toxicity, tense oedema, bullae, crepitus, skin anaesthesia or necrosis → **surgical emergency**: resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, urgent surgical debridement. Don't delay for imaging.

steps.title: Differentials
steps.body: DVT (Doppler), venous eczema (bilateral, itchy), gout.

- **Appearance & behaviour** (self-care, eye contact, psychomotor activity, rapport).
- **Speech** (rate, volume, tone, quantity).
- **Mood** (patient's words) and **affect** (observed: range, congruence).
- **Thought** form (e.g., flight of ideas, loosening) and content (delusions, overvalued ideas, obsessions, suicidal/homicidal ideation).
- **Perception** (hallucinations, illusions).
- **Cognition** (orientation, attention, memory).
- **Insight & judgement.**

steps.title: Communicate
steps.body: Private space, open questions, non-judgemental tone, normalising questions ('Some people in your situation hear voices…'), and always ask about risk.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Writing interpretations instead of observations; skipping risk; ignoring physical causes (thyroid, drugs, infections, delirium).

lessons.title: Lab: Screening for depression and anxiety

scenes.text: A 35-year-old teacher with poor sleep, low energy, loss of interest for 6 weeks.
Ask the two screening questions.

steps.title: Depression
steps.body: Core: persistently low mood and/or loss of interest/pleasure (anhedonia) for ≥ 2 weeks, plus symptoms like sleep and appetite change, fatigue, poor concentration, guilt/worthlessness, psychomotor change, suicidal thoughts. Tools such as PHQ-9 help screening and monitoring.

steps.title: Anxiety
steps.body: GAD: excessive worry most days for months with restlessness, tension, sleep disturbance; panic disorder: recurrent unexpected panic attacks. GAD-7 screens. Exclude physical causes (thyroid, caffeine, drugs, arrhythmia).

steps.title: Treatment principles
steps.body: Psychoeducation, psychological therapies (e.g., CBT), and medication by trained prescribers for moderate–severe illness; follow-up and risk review. Help numbers: Tele-MANAS 14416; emergency 112.

activity.prompt: Practise a depression screen with a peer (role-play).

Agree next steps and share help resources (Tele-MANAS 14416)

scenes.text: A 20-year-old engineering student believes classmates are controlling his thoughts through Wi-Fi; hears voices commenting.
Early treatment improves outcome.

steps.title: Recognise
steps.body: Delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech/behaviour, negative symptoms (withdrawal, flat affect, reduced motivation). Duration and pattern guide diagnosis (brief psychotic disorder, schizophrenia, mood disorder with psychotic features).

steps.title: Rule out organic causes
steps.body: Substances (cannabis, stimulants), delirium, epilepsy, infections (HIV, syphilis), thyroid, steroids, head injury, autoimmune encephalitis — history, exam and targeted tests.

steps.title: Engage
steps.body: Respectful, calm, avoid arguing with delusions, involve family with consent, refer to psychiatry/early-intervention services; assess risk.

steps.title: Psychiatric history
steps.body: Presenting complaint, history of presenting illness, past psychiatric and medical history, drug and substance history, family history, personal history (birth, childhood, education, work, relationships), premorbid personality, forensic history, social circumstances.

steps.title: Formulation
steps.body: Biopsychosocial: predisposing, precipitating, perpetuating and protective factors.

steps.title: Legal
steps.body: In India, admission and treatment follow the **Mental Healthcare Act 2017** (capacity, advance directives, nominated representative, rights). Follow local legal procedures.

scenes.text: A 22-year-old is medically stable after an intentional overdose.
A calm, non-judgemental conversation can save a life.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Assess
steps.body: Circumstances of the act (planning, isolation, precautions against discovery, final acts, note), intent, current suicidal thoughts and plans, access to means, hopelessness, mental illness, substance use, previous attempts, protective factors (family, beliefs, future plans), supports.

steps.title: Act
steps.body: Medical treatment first (including paracetamol levels after any overdose), observation level per risk, involve psychiatry, means restriction, collaborative **safety plan** (warning signs, coping steps, people to contact, professional numbers — Tele-MANAS 14416, emergency 112), family involvement with consent, follow-up within days.

steps.title: Language & law
steps.body: Avoid 'committed'/blaming language. In India, the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 directs that a person attempting suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and should receive care, not punishment.

Send home alone with a leaflet

end.text: She is reviewed by psychiatry, family remove stored medicines, and a safety plan with 14416/112 is written together.

lessons.title: Lab: Delirium vs dementia vs psychosis

scenes.text: An 80-year-old became confused overnight, pulling at lines, worse at night, after a UTI.
Delirium is a medical emergency.

steps.title: Delirium
steps.body: Acute onset, fluctuating course, **inattention**, disturbed consciousness/arousal, disorganised thinking; hyperactive, hypoactive (easily missed) or mixed. Screen with tools like 4AT or CAM.

steps.title: Causes & care
steps.body: Infection, drugs (anticholinergics, opioids, sedatives), withdrawal, metabolic (sodium, glucose, calcium), hypoxia, urinary retention, constipation, pain, stroke. Treat cause; non-drug care (orientation, family, glasses/hearing aids, sleep, hydration, mobilisation); avoid restraints; sedatives only for severe distress/risk at low doses per protocol.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: Dementia: gradual, progressive, attention usually preserved early. Primary psychosis: clear consciousness, attention usually intact.

activity.prompt: Delirium, dementia or primary psychosis?

options: Find and treat the underlying cause

scenes.text: A 30-year-old is shouting and pacing in the emergency department; staff are frightened.
Safety and dignity together.

steps.title: Approach
steps.body: Ensure safety (exits, help nearby, don't be alone), **verbal de-escalation**: calm voice, one person speaking, listen, acknowledge feelings, offer choices, reduce stimulation. Look for causes: hypoglycaemia, hypoxia, head injury, intoxication/withdrawal, delirium, psychosis, pain.

steps.title: Medication
steps.body: If de-escalation fails and risk is high, offer oral medication first; rapid tranquillisation per local protocol with monitoring (vitals, airway, ECG where indicated). Restraint only as a last resort, per law and protocol, with documentation.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Crowding the patient; arguing; missing a medical cause; inadequate monitoring after sedation.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — alcohol withdrawal on the ward

scenes.text: A 50-year-old admitted for a fracture is tremulous, sweaty, anxious and seeing insects on the wall 48 hours after his last drink.
Withdrawal can progress to seizures and delirium tremens.

steps.title: Timeline (typical)
steps.body: Tremor, anxiety, sweating within 6–24 h; withdrawal seizures around 12–48 h; **delirium tremens** around 48–72 h (confusion, hallucinations, autonomic instability) — a medical emergency.

steps.title: Management principles
steps.body: Assess with a withdrawal scale (e.g., CIWA-Ar), benzodiazepines per symptom-triggered or fixed protocol, **thiamine before glucose** (prevent Wernicke's encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia), fluids, electrolytes (Mg, K, phosphate), look for infection, head injury, hepatic encephalopathy; plan addiction support after recovery.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Not asking alcohol history at admission; giving glucose without thiamine in malnourished drinkers; under-dosing in severe withdrawal; missing a head injury.

uni-mbbs-emergency.title: MBBS Clinical · Emergency Medicine
uni-mbbs-emergency.description: Emergency medicine for MBBS students and interns: BLS and ALS algorithms as order-steps, anaphylaxis, shock and sepsis, Indian toxicology (organophosphates, snakebite, paracetamol) and ED triage — summarised in general terms from current international resuscitation guidance; always follow your local, up-to-date protocols. A study companion for MBBS students: it does not replace supervised clinical training or a licence.

courses.title: Resuscitation: BLS & ALS
courses.summary: Adult basic life support, AED use, the advanced life support algorithm, reversible causes and post-resuscitation care.
outcomes: Learners can order the adult BLS sequence
Learners can distinguish shockable from non-shockable rhythms
Learners can list the 4 Hs and 4 Ts
Learners can describe high-quality CPR

scenes.text: A visitor collapses in the OPD corridor and isn't moving.
Every minute without CPR reduces survival.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Sequence (general, per current international guidance)
steps.body: Check **danger** → check **response** (shake shoulders, shout) → **shout for help** → open **airway** (head tilt–chin lift) → check **breathing** for no more than 10 seconds (agonal gasps ≠ normal breathing) → **call 112 / hospital arrest team** and get an **AED** → start **chest compressions 30:2**.

steps.title: High-quality CPR
steps.body: Centre of chest, depth 5–6 cm, rate 100–120/min, full recoil, minimal interruptions, switch compressors about every 2 minutes. Attach AED as soon as it arrives and follow prompts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Mistaking agonal breathing for normal breathing; long pauses before shocks; leaning on the chest (incomplete recoil).

activity.prompt: Order the adult BLS sequence.
items: Ensure the scene is safe
Check for a response
Shout for help
Open the airway
Check for normal breathing (≤ 10 seconds)
Call 112 / arrest team and send for an AED
Start 30 compressions then 2 breaths, continue
Attach AED and follow its prompts

quiz.q: Agonal gasps should be treated as

scenes.text: The arrest team attaches pads. The rhythm is a chaotic irregular waveform without QRS complexes.
Analyse, decide, minimise pauses.

steps.title: Rhythms
steps.body:
**Shockable:** ventricular fibrillation (chaotic, no organised QRS), pulseless ventricular tachycardia (broad regular complexes without pulse).
**Non-shockable:** asystole (flat line — check leads and gain), pulseless electrical activity (organised rhythm without a pulse).

steps.title: ALS loop (general)
steps.body: CPR 2-minute cycles; rhythm check; shock if VF/pVT then immediately resume CPR; IV/IO access; adrenaline 1 mg every 3–5 minutes (non-shockable: as soon as access; shockable: after the 3rd shock); amiodarone after the 3rd shock for VF/pVT; airway and capnography; treat reversible causes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Pulse checks that take too long; stopping compressions while charging the defibrillator (continue until ready); forgetting reversible causes.

activity.prompt: Classify the rhythm in cardiac arrest.

items.text: Pulseless electrical activity (sinus rhythm on monitor, no pulse)
Flat line confirmed with correct leads and gain

lessons.title: Lab: Reversible causes — 4 Hs and 4 Ts

scenes.text: During CPR, the team leader asks: 'What could have caused this?'
Treating the cause gives the best chance.

steps.title: 4 Hs
steps.body: **Hypoxia**, **Hypovolaemia**, **Hypo/hyperkalaemia** and other metabolic, **Hypothermia** (and hyperthermia).

steps.title: 4 Ts
steps.body: **Thrombosis** (coronary or pulmonary), **Tension pneumothorax**, **Tamponade** (cardiac), **Toxins**.

steps.title: Clues
steps.body: Point-of-care ultrasound (without interrupting CPR), ABG/VBG for K, history from bystanders, drug chart, recent surgery (PE), trauma (tension, tamponade, hypovolaemia).

steps.title: Roles
steps.body: Team leader, compressors (rotate), airway, defibrillator/monitor, drugs/IV access, recorder (times, drugs, shocks). Closed-loop communication.

steps.title: After ROSC
steps.body: ABCDE, oxygen targeting SpO2 94–98%, avoid hypotension, 12-lead ECG (PCI if STEMI), glucose control, temperature control (avoid fever), ICU transfer, family update.

steps.title: Ethics
steps.body: Check for a documented do-not-attempt-CPR decision; communicate with family compassionately; debrief the team.

courses.title: Shock, anaphylaxis & sepsis
courses.summary: Recognising and treating anaphylaxis, the types of shock, and the sepsis first hour.
outcomes: Learners can recognise anaphylaxis and give first-line treatment per protocol
Learners can classify shock types
Learners can apply the qSOFA concept and sepsis bundle
Learners can calculate MAP

lessons.title: Lab: Case — anaphylaxis after an injection

scenes.text: Minutes after an IV antibiotic, a patient develops wheeze, lip swelling, hives and BP 80/50.
Anaphylaxis — adrenaline.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Recognise
steps.body: Sudden onset airway (swelling, stridor, hoarseness) and/or breathing (wheeze, hypoxia) and/or circulation (hypotension, collapse) problems, usually with skin/mucosal changes (which may be absent), after a likely trigger.

steps.title: Treat (general, per resuscitation guidance)
steps.body: Stop the trigger, call for help, **IM adrenaline** into the anterolateral thigh (adult dose per protocol — commonly 0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL (1:1000)), repeat after about 5 minutes if no improvement, lie flat (sit up if breathing difficulty; left lateral if pregnant), high-flow oxygen, IV fluid bolus for shock, monitor; refractory → senior/ICU for adrenaline infusion. Antihistamines/steroids are not first-line.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Giving antihistamine first and delaying adrenaline; IV adrenaline bolus by non-experts; standing the patient up; early discharge without observation and allergy documentation.

s1.text: Wheeze, lip swelling, hives, BP 80/50 after IV antibiotic.

choices.label: Stop the drug, call for help, IM adrenaline in the anterolateral thigh per protocol
IV antihistamine and wait
Sit the patient up and walk to the bed

s2.text: Five minutes later: still hypotensive and wheezy.

choices.label: Repeat IM adrenaline, IV fluid bolus, high-flow oxygen, escalate to senior/ICU
Discharge

end.text: She improves. You document the allergy prominently, observe her, and arrange allergy referral and adrenaline auto-injector training if indicated.

quiz.q: Repeat IM adrenaline if no improvement after about

scenes.text: Four hypotensive patients: bleeding, MI, sepsis, and tension pneumothorax.
Different mechanisms, different treatments.

steps.title: Classification
steps.body:
- **Hypovolaemic:** haemorrhage, dehydration — cold peripheries, low JVP.
- **Cardiogenic:** pump failure (MI, arrhythmia) — cold, high JVP, pulmonary oedema.
- **Distributive:** sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic — often warm peripheries early, low systemic vascular resistance.
- **Obstructive:** tension pneumothorax, tamponade, massive PE — high JVP, clear lungs (except PE).

steps.title: MAP
steps.body: Mean arterial pressure ≈ DBP + ⅓(SBP − DBP). BP 90/60 → 60 + 10 = 70 mmHg. Sepsis targets often use MAP ≥ 65 mmHg.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Fluid-loading cardiogenic shock; missing obstructive causes that need a procedure.

activity.prompt: Classify each shocked patient.

items.text: Large anterior MI with pulmonary oedema
Pneumonia with warm peripheries and low BP

quiz.q: Raised JVP, clear lungs, hypotension after chest trauma

scenes.text: An 80-year-old with UTI symptoms: confused, RR 24, systolic BP 95.
Sepsis: life-threatening organ dysfunction due to dysregulated response to infection.

steps.title: Screen
steps.body: **qSOFA** (prognostic prompt, not a diagnosis): RR ≥ 22, altered mentation, SBP ≤ 100 — ≥ 2 suggests higher risk. Use your hospital's sepsis screening and early warning scores.

steps.title: Bundle (general)
steps.body: Measure lactate; blood cultures **before** antibiotics (without delaying them); broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly (within 1 hour for suspected septic shock/high risk); IV crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L; vasopressors if hypotension persists to target MAP ≥ 65 mmHg; source control; urine output monitoring.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Waiting for culture results; missing hypothermia as a sepsis sign; forgetting source control (drain the abscess, remove the infected line).

activity.prompt: Calculate the qSOFA score: RR 24, confused, systolic BP 95 mmHg.

scenes.text: A 55-year-old with pneumonia: BP 82/45 after 30 mL/kg fluids, lactate 5.2, urine 10 mL/h.
Escalate.

steps.title: Next steps
steps.body: Senior/ICU review, vasopressor (noradrenaline per protocol, ideally via central line — peripheral initially in some protocols), arterial line, repeat lactate, reassess fluid responsiveness, review antibiotic choice and source, consider steroids if refractory per protocol.

steps.title: Fluid volume
steps.body: A common initial guide is 30 mL/kg crystalloid in sepsis-induced hypotension, then reassess (individualise for heart failure/renal disease).

steps.title: Communicate
steps.body: Update family; discuss goals of care when appropriate.

courses.title: Toxicology in Indian emergency departments
courses.summary: Organophosphate poisoning, snakebite envenomation and paracetamol overdose — recognition and principles of care.
outcomes: Learners can recognise the cholinergic toxidrome and its treatment principles
Learners can manage snakebite first aid and ASV indications in principle
Learners can calculate ingested paracetamol dose per kg
Learners can apply a general approach to the poisoned patient

lessons.title: Lab: General approach to the poisoned patient

scenes.text: A 19-year-old brought in drowsy; family found an empty container.
ABC first, then the toxin.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Approach
steps.body: ABCDE with glucose; history (what, how much, when, route, co-ingestants, intent); examination for toxidromes; ECG; bloods including paracetamol and salicylate levels when relevant; contact poison information service; decontamination only when indicated (e.g., activated charcoal within a window if airway protected, per guidance); specific antidotes; supportive care; psychiatric assessment once medically fit.

steps.title: Toxidromes
steps.body:
- **Cholinergic:** salivation, lacrimation, urination, diarrhoea, bronchorrhoea, bradycardia, miosis.
- **Anticholinergic:** hot, dry, flushed, mydriasis, delirium, urinary retention.
- **Opioid:** miosis, respiratory depression, reduced consciousness.
- **Sympathomimetic:** agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis, sweating.

steps.title: Self-harm
steps.body: Treat with dignity; intentional poisoning needs a psychiatric risk assessment and support (Tele-MANAS 14416).

activity.prompt: Match the toxidrome.

items.text: Hot dry skin, dilated pupils, delirium
Urinary retention and absent bowel sounds

quiz.q: Hot, dry, flushed, mydriatic and delirious

options: A protected airway and indication within a time window

quiz.q: After medical stabilisation in intentional poisoning

scenes.text: A farmer ingested an organophosphate pesticide: drooling, vomiting, sweating, pinpoint pupils, wheeze, HR 48.
Atropinise to dry secretions.

steps.title: Mechanism
steps.body: Inhibition of acetylcholinesterase → excess acetylcholine at muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS receptors.

steps.title: Management principles
steps.body: Decontaminate (remove clothes, wash skin — staff use protection), ABC with early airway control if needed; **atropine** titrated (doubling doses per protocol) to clear chest secretions, HR > 80, SBP > 80, dry axillae — **not** to pupil size; pralidoxime per local protocol; benzodiazepines for seizures; ICU monitoring for respiratory failure and **intermediate syndrome** (proximal weakness 1–4 days later).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using pupil dilation as the atropine endpoint; under-atropinising; missing delayed respiratory weakness; succinylcholine prolonged effect.

s1.text: Drooling, wheeze with crackles, HR 48, BP 80/50, pinpoint pupils.

choices.label: Protect staff, decontaminate, ABC, IV atropine titrated to chest secretions, HR and BP

s2.text: After atropinisation: chest clear, HR 95, BP 110/70, axillae dry. Day 3: neck flexion weakness and falling vital capacity.

choices.label: Suspect intermediate syndrome — ICU review for ventilatory support
Discharge

end.text: He is ventilated briefly and recovers; a psychiatric assessment and family support follow.

options: Clear chest, HR > 80, SBP > 80, dry axillae

lessons.title: Lab: Snakebite — first aid and ASV

scenes.text: A 30-year-old was bitten on the foot at night while walking in a field.
Gums bleeding 2 hours later.

steps.title: First aid
steps.body: Reassure, immobilise the limb, remove rings/tight items, transport quickly to a facility with anti-snake venom (ASV) — call 112. **Avoid** cutting, sucking, tight tourniquets, ice, herbal remedies.

steps.title: Hospital
steps.body: Assess envenomation: local swelling; **haemotoxic** (bleeding, 20-minute whole blood clotting test — unclotted suggests coagulopathy; typical of Russell's viper/saw-scaled viper); **neurotoxic** (ptosis, ophthalmoplegia, bulbar and respiratory weakness — cobra, krait; krait bites may be painless at night). Give polyvalent ASV when signs of systemic envenomation are present per national protocol; watch for ASV reactions (adrenaline ready); neostigmine trial and ventilation for neurotoxicity as indicated; dialysis for AKI.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Giving ASV without envenomation signs; tourniquets; missing painless krait bites in a sleeping person with abdominal pain and ptosis.

items: Reassure and immobilise the bitten limb; remove rings
Transport urgently to a facility with ASV (call 112)
ABC assessment and IV access on arrival
Assess for local and systemic envenomation including 20-minute whole blood clotting test
Give polyvalent ASV if systemic envenomation, with adrenaline ready
Monitor for neurotoxicity, bleeding and AKI; repeat WBCT per protocol

options: There are signs of systemic envenomation

scenes.text: A 20-year-old (60 kg) took 20 tablets of 500 mg paracetamol 5 hours ago after an exam.
Calculate and plan.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Paracetamol overdose can cause **liver failure** days later, even when the patient initially feels well. The antidote **N-acetylcysteine (NAC)** is highly effective, best within 8 hours of ingestion.

steps.title: Approach
steps.body: Time of ingestion, amount (mg/kg), staggered vs single, risk factors. Single acute ingestion with known time: paracetamol level at ≥ 4 hours plotted on the treatment nomogram per local guideline; start NAC immediately if presentation is ≥ 8 h with significant ingestion, staggered/unknown time, or liver injury. Monitor LFT, INR, creatinine, glucose; liver unit referral if criteria met. Psychiatric assessment after.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Taking a level before 4 hours for a single acute ingestion; delaying NAC past 8 hours waiting for a level; discharging without mental health assessment.

This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

steps.title: Triage principles
steps.body: Rapid assessment of airway, breathing, circulation, disability, vital signs and key complaints, assigning priority (e.g., red immediate, orange very urgent, yellow urgent, green standard, blue non-urgent — systems vary). Re-triage if condition changes.

steps.title: Discriminators
steps.body: Airway compromise, shock, unresponsiveness, active seizure, severe pain, chest pain with features of ACS, stroke signs, sepsis signs, pregnancy with bleeding.

steps.title: Common mistakes

steps.title: ABCDE
steps.body: **A**: talking? noises? obstruction? → open airway, suction, adjuncts. **B**: RR, SpO2, chest movement, auscultation → oxygen, bronchodilators, decompress. **C**: HR, BP, CRT, ECG, IV access, bloods → fluids, stop bleeding. **D**: AVPU/GCS, pupils, glucose → treat hypoglycaemia. **E**: expose, temperature, rash, wounds, calves.

steps.title: Reassess
steps.body: After each intervention reassess; call for help early; communicate clearly.

steps.title: Glucose
steps.body: Always check capillary glucose in altered consciousness or seizures.

steps.title: SBAR
steps.body: **S**ituation: who and what now. **B**ackground: admission reason, relevant history. **A**ssessment: vitals, findings, your impression. **R**ecommendation: what needs doing, by when, and escalation triggers.

steps.title: Example
steps.body: 'S: Mr Kumar, bed 12, 70, new hypotension 85/50. B: Day 2 after bowel resection, diabetic. A: HR 120, febrile, abdomen more tender — I'm concerned about anastomotic leak/sepsis; given fluid bolus, cultures and antibiotics. R: Please review within 15 minutes; CT arranged; call ICU if MAP < 65 after second bolus.'

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Long unstructured stories; no clear request; no time frame.

courses.title: Thanatology · Death & Post-mortem Changes
courses.summary: Definitions of death, early and late post-mortem changes, estimating time since death, and the medico-legal importance of each change — described clinically and respectfully.
outcomes: Learners can distinguish somatic, molecular and brain-stem death
Learners can describe algor, livor and rigor mortis and their timing
Learners can estimate time since death with stated uncertainty
Learners can recognise medico-legally important colour changes and cadaveric spasm

scenes.text: On night duty, a nurse calls you to certify a patient's death.
You must confirm death carefully and respectfully, then inform the family.
What exactly do you check?

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Types of death
steps.body:
- **Somatic (clinical) death**: irreversible cessation of circulation and respiration (and brain function).
- **Molecular (cellular) death**: death of individual cells, occurring over hours after somatic death — the basis of post-mortem changes and organ donation timing.
- **Brain-stem death**: irreversible loss of brain-stem function with the heart beating on a ventilator; certified by a designated medical board using formal criteria under India's transplantation law.
- **Suspended animation**: apparent death (drowning, electrocution, hypothermia) — resuscitation may succeed, so assess carefully.

steps.title: Confirming death
steps.body: Absence of a central pulse and heart sounds and of breath sounds over a sustained period of observation (per local protocol), fixed dilated pupils, no response to painful stimulus. Document date and time, and inform the senior and family with compassion. Unnatural or suspicious deaths are **medico-legal cases** and must be reported to the police.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Certifying too quickly in hypothermia, drowning or drug overdose — 'not dead until warm and dead' guides resuscitation in hypothermia.
- Issuing a death certificate for an unnatural death instead of informing the police.

story.title: The body in the rented room

scenes.text: Police call the forensic team to a rented room. A man is found dead in bed.
Rectal temperature 89.4 °F, rigor fully developed, lividity fixed.
Estimate the time since death — with honesty about uncertainty.

steps.title: Algor mortis (cooling)
steps.body: A rough Indian textbook rule: hours since death ≈ (98.4 − rectal temperature in °F) ÷ 1.5. It is highly variable: body size, clothing, ambient temperature, fever before death and air movement all change the rate. In hot climates the body may cool slowly or not at all.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body:
Rectal 89.4 °F: (98.4 − 89.4) ÷ 1.5 = 9 ÷ 1.5 = **6 hours** (rough).
Combine with other signs: fixed lividity (after ~6–8 h) and fully developed rigor (~12 h in temperate conditions; faster in heat) → a window of roughly 6–12 hours. Always report a **range**, not a single number.

steps.title: Livor and rigor
steps.body:
- **Livor mortis (hypostasis)**: purple-red discolouration of dependent parts, appearing within about an hour, becoming **fixed** at about 6–8 h (shifting no longer occurs). Absent over pressure points (contact pallor).
- **Rigor mortis**: stiffening from ATP depletion; begins about 1–2 h after death, follows **Nysten's rule** (eyelids, face, neck, then downwards), passes off in the same order. Speeded by heat and exertion before death.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Giving an exact time of death — courts need an honest range.
- Confusing hypostasis with bruising — a bruise has extravasated blood that doesn't wash out on incision.

lessons.title: Lab: Clinical case — colour of lividity and cadaveric spasm

scenes.text: Scene 1: a couple found in a car parked in a closed garage with the engine running.
Scene 2: a man found with a knife tightly gripped in his hand.
Each finding has medico-legal meaning.

steps.title: Colour clues
steps.body:
- **Cherry-red** hypostasis: carbon monoxide poisoning (carboxyhaemoglobin); also bright pink in cyanide poisoning and in cold exposure.
- **Chocolate/brown**: methaemoglobin-forming poisons (nitrites, chlorates, some aniline compounds).
- Usual: purple-red.

steps.title: Cadaveric spasm
steps.body: **Instantaneous rigor** at the moment of death, affecting a group of muscles, usually in violent death with intense emotion. A weapon firmly gripped in the hand by cadaveric spasm suggests the person was holding it at death — it cannot be reproduced by putting a weapon in a dead hand later. Rare; must be distinguished from ordinary rigor.

steps.title: Respect
steps.body: Treat the deceased and their family with dignity. Preserve evidence, document carefully, and leave interpretation to the forensic expert at autopsy.

Announce your conclusion to the media

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — sort early and late post-mortem changes

scenes.text: The examiner lists post-mortem changes and asks: early or late?
Late changes include decomposition and modified forms like adipocere.

steps.title: Late changes
steps.body:
- **Putrefaction**: bacterial decomposition; first visible sign in India is usually a **greenish discolouration of the right iliac fossa** (caecum close to the skin) within about a day, then marbling, bloating, skin slippage. Faster in heat.
- **Adipocere** (saponification): waxy change in moist, warm environments (bodies in water/damp soil) over weeks.
- **Mummification**: drying in hot, dry, airy conditions; preserves features.

Early changes: pallor, loss of corneal lustre/clouding, **tache noire** (eyes open), algor, livor, rigor.

steps.title: Legal note
steps.body: This is general education, not legal advice. Laws, rules and section numbers change — always follow the current text of the law, your institution's medico-legal protocol and senior guidance. India's criminal codes are now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS) and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), in force from 1 July 2024 (replacing the IPC, CrPC and Indian Evidence Act).

scenes.text: A man arrives after a fight. He has a graze, a bruise, a split eyebrow and a clean cut on his forearm.
Each injury type tells a story about the weapon.
Name each one precisely.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Blunt-force injuries
steps.body:
- **Abrasion**: loss of superficial epidermis (graze, scratch, pressure abrasion); shows direction of force; heals without scar.
- **Contusion (bruise)**: bleeding into tissues with intact skin; colour changes over days (red/purple → blue → green → yellow) but ageing bruises by colour is **unreliable**; may appear away from the impact site.
- **Laceration**: tearing of skin by blunt force — irregular, bruised margins, **tissue bridges** in the depth, hair roots crushed; common over bony areas (scalp, eyebrow).

steps.title: Sharp-force injuries
steps.body:
- **Incised wound**: clean-cut, **longer than deep**, clean margins, no tissue bridges; bleeds freely.
- **Stab wound**: **deeper than long**; shape may suggest single- or double-edged blade.
- **Chop wound**: heavy sharp weapon (axe) — features of both cutting and crushing.
- **Defence wounds**: on forearms and palms while warding off an attack — suggest homicide.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a split over the eyebrow from a punch an 'incised wound' — it is a laceration (tissue bridges).
- Stating the exact age of a bruise from colour alone.

steps.title: Firearm wounds (overview)
steps.body: **Entry wound** (rifled weapon, distant range): usually smaller, round, inverted margins with an **abrasion collar**; at close range there may be burning, blackening (smoke) and **tattooing** (unburnt powder). **Exit wound**: usually larger, irregular, everted, no collar or tattooing. Shotgun patterns depend on range (pellet spread). Range estimation and wound interpretation are for the forensic expert.

steps.title: Opinion language
steps.body: Say 'consistent with' rather than 'caused by'. E.g. 'The injury is consistent with a blow from a hard blunt object.'

steps.title: Ligature mark comparison
steps.body:
**Hanging** (usually suicidal): mark **oblique**, **above the thyroid cartilage**, **incomplete/non-continuous** (gap at the knot), base often parchment-like; salivary dribbling from the angle of the mouth may be seen; fracture of hyoid more likely in older people.

**Ligature strangulation** (usually homicidal): mark **horizontal**, **at or below the thyroid cartilage**, **complete/continuous**, with more bruising and signs of struggle; congestion and petechiae of face are more marked.

These are typical patterns, not absolute rules — the full autopsy and scene investigation decide.

courses.summary: General management of poisoning, snake bite, paracetamol overdose, corrosives, aluminium phosphide and heavy metals — principles only, with escalation and the medico-legal duties of the doctor.

lessons.title: General approach to the poisoned patient

scenes.text: A 24-year-old is brought drowsy with an empty strip of tablets.
The family doesn't know what or when.
Start with a system that works for any poison.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Steps
steps.body:
1. **Resuscitate**: airway, breathing, circulation, glucose check, seizures.
2. **History** from patient/family/strip/bottle; time and amount; intent.
3. **Examine** for a toxidrome: cholinergic (secretions, miosis), anticholinergic (hot, dry, flushed, dilated pupils, delirium, urinary retention), opioid (miosis, respiratory depression, coma), sympathomimetic (tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, mydriasis, sweating).
4. **Decontaminate** when appropriate (activated charcoal for some ingestions, within limits, airway protected; skin washing; **no** induced vomiting for corrosives/hydrocarbons).
5. **Antidotes** where they exist (naloxone for opioids, atropine/oximes for OPs, N-acetylcysteine for paracetamol, fomepizole/ethanol for methanol, antivenom).
6. **Supportive care**, monitoring, and **psychiatric assessment** in self-harm.
7. **Medico-legal**: poisoning is a medico-legal case — inform the police per protocol, preserve samples (gastric lavage/vomit, blood, urine).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Inducing vomiting after corrosive or kerosene ingestion.
- Forgetting to check blood glucose in every drowsy patient.

lessons.title: Lab: Clinical case — snake bite in the field

scenes.text: A farmer is bitten on the foot while walking in a paddy field at night.
He didn't see the snake.
First aid, then hospital — step by step.

steps.title: Envenomation types (India's 'big four')
steps.body:
- **Neurotoxic** — cobra, krait: ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, descending paralysis, respiratory failure. **Krait** bites often happen at night while sleeping on the floor, may be painless with minimal local signs.
- **Haemotoxic/vasculotoxic** — Russell's viper, saw-scaled viper: local swelling, bleeding gums, haematuria, incoagulable blood; Russell's viper also causes acute kidney injury.

**20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT)**: blood in a clean dry glass tube left undisturbed 20 min — no clot suggests viper envenomation. **Polyvalent anti-snake venom (ASV)** covers the big four; given in hospital when envenomation signs appear, with readiness to treat reactions.

steps.title: First aid
steps.body: Reassure, keep the person still, **immobilise the bitten limb** like a fracture, remove rings/tight items, transport to hospital quickly (call 112). **Do not** cut, suck, apply ice, tourniquets or herbal remedies.

steps.title: Emergency
steps.body: Every snake bite should go to a hospital that stocks ASV, even if the person feels well — signs can appear hours later.

s0.text: Farmer bitten at night in a paddy field. What is the right first aid?

choices.label: Reassure, immobilise the limb, remove tight items and transport quickly to hospital

s1.text: At hospital, his foot is swollen and his gums bleed; 20WBCT shows no clot. Envenomation type?

choices.label: Haemotoxic — likely a viper
Neurotoxic — likely a krait

s2.text: What is the specific treatment?

choices.label: Polyvalent anti-snake venom in hospital, with monitoring and readiness for reactions, per protocol
choices.feedback: And repeat 20WBCT to guide further doses.

choices.label: Antibiotics alone

choices.label: Acute kidney injury — escalate to the senior/nephrology team
choices.feedback: Common after Russell's viper bites; may need dialysis.

choices.label: Normal recovery
choices.feedback: Falling urine output is a warning sign.

end.text: Excellent: correct first aid, viper identified by 20WBCT, ASV given and AKI escalated.

lessons.title: Lab: Sort the poisons and their signs

scenes.text: The forensic museum displays specimens from different poisonings.
Each poison leaves its own clues.
Sort the signs.

steps.title: Clues
steps.body:
- **Paracetamol overdose**: few early symptoms; liver injury after 24–72 h; antidote **N-acetylcysteine** (replenishes glutathione); treatment decided using timed blood levels and a nomogram by the treating team.
- **Aluminium phosphide** (rice tablets): releases phosphine gas — shock, arrhythmias, high mortality; no specific antidote; supportive ICU care.
- **Arsenic (chronic)**: raindrop pigmentation, palmar/plantar hyperkeratosis, **Mees' lines** on nails, neuropathy — e.g. contaminated groundwater in parts of eastern India.
- **Lead (chronic)**: **Burton's line** on gums, basophilic stippling of red cells, abdominal colic, wrist drop, anaemia, cognitive effects in children.
- **Methanol**: visual blurring ('snowfield' vision), high anion gap acidosis.
- **Corrosives (acids/alkalis)**: burns of mouth and oesophagus; risk of perforation and later strictures.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Valid informed consent
steps.body:
- Given by a person with **capacity**, **voluntarily**, after being told in understandable language about the **nature, purpose, benefits, risks, alternatives** (including no treatment), and who will do it.
- **Types**: implied (rolling up a sleeve for a BP check), expressed oral, expressed written (surgery, procedures, research).
- **Exceptions/special cases**: emergencies where delay threatens life and no one can consent (act in best interests, document); minors and those lacking capacity (guardian consent); therapeutic privilege is very limited.
- **Confidentiality**: duty to keep patient information private; exceptions include legal requirements (notifiable diseases, court orders, medico-legal cases), and serious risk to others.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A signature on a blank form is not informed consent.
- Consent for one procedure doesn't cover a different, non-urgent one discovered during surgery.

steps.title: Medical negligence
steps.body: Four elements (the '4 Ds'): **Duty** of care existed; **Dereliction** — breach of the standard expected of a reasonably competent doctor (the Bolam test, applied in India with refinements); **Direct causation** — the breach caused the harm; **Damage** occurred. A bad outcome alone is not negligence. Doctors can face civil liability (including consumer forums), and criminal liability only for gross negligence. Good notes, informed consent and timely referral are the best protection.

steps.title: Res ipsa loquitur
steps.body: 'The thing speaks for itself' — e.g. a swab left inside the abdomen, or operating on the wrong limb; the burden shifts to the doctor to explain.

steps.title: Dying declaration
steps.body: A statement by a person about the cause or circumstances of their death, admissible as evidence under the **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam** (successor to the Evidence Act). Ideally recorded by a **magistrate**; if no time, by a doctor or other person. The doctor **certifies that the declarant is conscious and mentally fit (compos mentis)** before and after recording; uses the person's own words; questions and answers recorded verbatim; signed/thumb-printed and witnessed.

steps.title: Inquest
steps.body: An inquiry into the cause of an unnatural or suspicious death. In India, the **police inquest** is the most common; **magistrate inquest** is mandatory in certain situations such as deaths in police or judicial custody, and deaths of women within seven years of marriage in suspicious circumstances (under the BNSS). The autopsy surgeon provides the medical cause of death.

steps.title: Key laws (general terms)
steps.body:
- **POCSO Act, 2012**: any sexual offence against a child (under 18) must be **reported** to the police or Special Juvenile Police Unit; failure to report is an offence. Examination with consent of the child/guardian, child-friendly, by a woman doctor for girls where required; treatment comes first. (Age of consent is 18.)
- **MTP Act, 1971 (amended 2021)**: termination by a registered medical practitioner up to 20 weeks on one provider's opinion; 20–24 weeks for specified categories with two providers; beyond that only for substantial fetal abnormalities via a medical board. Confidentiality of the woman is protected.
- **Notifiable diseases** (e.g. TB): notify the public health authority.
- **Medico-legal cases** (injuries, burns, poisoning, suspicious deaths): inform the police.

lessons.title: Lab: Case — crushing chest pain in casualty

scenes.text: A 58-year-old diabetic smoker arrives with 40 minutes of central chest heaviness radiating to the left arm, sweating.
The intern knows: in suspected ACS, time is myocardium. A 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of arrival.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Focused history
steps.body:
- **Site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms** (sweating, nausea, breathlessness), timing, exacerbating/relieving, severity.
- Risk factors: diabetes, smoking, hypertension, dyslipidaemia, family history of premature CAD.
- Diabetics, women and the elderly may present atypically (breathlessness, epigastric discomfort, fatigue).

steps.title: Spectrum of ACS
steps.body:
- **STEMI:** ST elevation in two contiguous leads (or new LBBB with a convincing story) → immediate reperfusion.
- **NSTEMI:** troponin rise without ST elevation; ECG may show ST depression or T inversion.
- **Unstable angina:** ischaemic pain, troponin not raised.

Differentials you must not miss: aortic dissection, pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, pericarditis, oesophageal rupture.

steps.title: Initial management (general principles)
steps.body: Oxygen only if saturation is low, aspirin (unless contraindicated), antianginal therapy as per protocol, analgesia, anticoagulation and reperfusion — primary PCI if available in time, otherwise thrombolysis per local protocol. Always activate the cath-lab/senior pathway early. Drug doses come from your hospital protocol, not memory.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Waiting for troponin before acting on a clear STEMI ECG.
- Giving thrombolysis without excluding aortic dissection signs (tearing pain to back, pulse/BP difference between arms).
- Discharging a 'normal ECG' patient without serial ECGs and troponins.

A system — rate, rhythm, axis, intervals, morphology — stops you missing things.

steps.title: A systematic read
steps.body:
1. Patient details, date, calibration (10 mm/mV, 25 mm/s).
2. **Rate:** 300 ÷ number of large squares between R waves (regular), or count QRS in 10 s strip × 6.
3. **Rhythm:** P before every QRS? regular?
4. **Axis:** leads I and aVF positive = normal.
5. **Intervals:** PR 120–200 ms; QRS < 120 ms; QTc.
6. **Morphology:** ST, T, Q waves, hypertrophy, bundle branch block.

steps.title: Patterns described
steps.body:
- **AF:** irregularly irregular, no P waves, fibrillatory baseline.
- **Hyperkalaemia:** tall peaked T waves → flattened P, wide QRS → sine-wave.
- **Complete heart block:** P waves and QRS dissociated, slow escape rhythm.
- **LBBB:** QRS ≥ 120 ms, broad notched R in V6, deep S in V1.

steps.title: QTc by Bazett
steps.body: QTc = QT ÷ √RR (RR in seconds). Example: QT 400 ms, HR 90 → RR = 60/90 = 0.667 s → √0.667 = 0.816 → QTc ≈ 490 ms (prolonged).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the machine's auto-report as the diagnosis.
- Forgetting to compare with an old ECG.
- Missing hyperkalaemia because the patient 'looks fine'.

scenes.text: A 22-year-old known asthmatic arrives wheezing, speaking in words, RR 30, HR 120.
Peak flow 40% of best. The team must act fast.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Grade severity (general)
steps.body:
- **Moderate:** PEF > 50–75% best, speech normal.
- **Acute severe:** PEF 33–50%, RR ≥ 25, HR ≥ 110, can't complete sentences.
- **Life-threatening:** PEF < 33%, SpO2 < 92%, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, arrhythmia, hypotension, altered consciousness, 'normal' PaCO2.
- **Near-fatal:** raised PaCO2 or needing ventilation.

steps.title: Management principles
steps.body: Oxygen to target 94–98%, repeated or back-to-back nebulised short-acting β2-agonist, nebulised ipratropium in severe cases, systemic corticosteroid early, consider IV magnesium in severe/life-threatening per protocol, and early ICU/anaesthesia involvement if life-threatening features.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: A 'normal' PaCO2 in a breathless asthmatic is a danger sign (tiring). Sedatives are contraindicated. Don't discharge without inhaler technique check and steroid course.

s1.text: SpO2 91%, speaking in words, PEF 40%. First action?

Order chest X-ray and wait

choices.feedback: Sedation can stop breathing in asthma.

s2.text: After 2 nebs: silent chest developing, ABG PaCO2 rising to 'normal' 5.5 kPa (41 mmHg).

choices.label: Life-threatening — call ICU/anaesthesia urgently, add ipratropium and IV magnesium per protocol
Reassure: PaCO2 is normal
choices.feedback: In acute asthma, normal PaCO2 = exhaustion.

choices.label: Send home with inhaler

lessons.title: Lab: ABG interpretation in five steps

scenes.text: pH 7.21, PaCO2 24 mmHg, HCO3 10 mmol/L, Na 138, Cl 100.
A five-step method turns numbers into a diagnosis.

steps.title: Five steps
steps.body:
1. **pH:** < 7.35 acidaemia; > 7.45 alkalaemia.
2. **Primary process:** PaCO2 (normal 35–45 mmHg) or HCO3 (22–26).
3. **Compensation:** metabolic acidosis → expected PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3 + 8 (± 2) (Winter's formula).
4. **Anion gap** = Na − (Cl + HCO3); normal about 8–12 (lab dependent).
5. **Oxygenation:** PaO2 vs FiO2; clinical context.

steps.title: Solved example
steps.body: pH 7.21 → acidaemia. HCO3 10 low → metabolic acidosis. Expected PaCO2 = 1.5×10 + 8 = 23 ± 2 → measured 24 → appropriately compensated. AG = 138 − (100 + 10) = 28 → high anion gap metabolic acidosis (e.g. DKA, lactic acidosis, renal failure, toxins).

steps.title: Causes to remember
steps.body:
- **High AG:** ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, uraemia, methanol/ethylene glycol, salicylate.
- **Normal AG (hyperchloraemic):** diarrhoea, renal tubular acidosis, large saline infusion.
- **Respiratory acidosis:** COPD exacerbation, opioid overdose, neuromuscular weakness.
- **Metabolic alkalosis:** vomiting, diuretics.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Calling compensation 'complete'; forgetting albumin lowers the anion gap; ignoring a mixed disorder when PaCO2 falls outside Winter's range.

scenes.text: A 66-year-old with COPD: increased breathlessness and purulent sputum; drowsy.

steps.title: Interpret
steps.body: pH 7.28 acidaemia, PaCO2 high → respiratory acidosis; HCO3 31 is raised → partial metabolic compensation suggesting chronic retention, now acute-on-chronic. Drowsiness with hypercapnia = CO2 narcosis risk.

steps.body: Controlled oxygen to target 88–92% (Venturi), bronchodilators, systemic steroid, antibiotics if purulent sputum, and **non-invasive ventilation** for persistent respiratory acidosis (pH < 7.35 with PaCO2 > 45 mmHg) after initial treatment. scenes.text: A type 1 diabetic student stopped insulin during a stomach bug; now drowsy and breathing deeply.
Glucose 26 mmol/L, ketones 5.2 mmol/L, pH 7.12, HCO3 9.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Diagnosis (common criteria)
steps.body: Ketonaemia ≥ 3 mmol/L (or significant ketonuria), glucose > 11 mmol/L or known diabetes, and venous pH < 7.3 and/or bicarbonate < 15 mmol/L. Kussmaul breathing, ketotic breath, dehydration, abdominal pain.

steps.title: Management principles
steps.body: IV fluid resuscitation with 0.9% saline, fixed-rate IV insulin infusion per protocol, potassium replacement guided by levels (insulin drives K into cells), hourly glucose/ketones, 2-hourly VBG and potassium, add glucose when blood glucose falls below a threshold while insulin continues, find and treat the precipitant. Senior and critical-care input if pH very low, GCS reduced or shock.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Stopping insulin when glucose normalises (ketones still high); forgetting potassium; over-rapid fluids in children (cerebral oedema risk — use paediatric protocol).

steps.title: Why it kills
steps.body: High extracellular K depolarises myocytes → conduction slowing → bradycardia, VF or asystole. ECG changes need immediate treatment.

steps.title: Three-part plan
steps.body:
1. **Protect the heart:** IV calcium (gluconate or chloride per protocol) if ECG changes.
2. **Shift K into cells:** insulin–glucose infusion; nebulised salbutamol as adjunct.
3. **Remove K:** stop K-raising drugs, binders, diuretics if appropriate, **dialysis** for refractory cases.
Recheck K and glucose (risk of hypoglycaemia after insulin).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Haemolysed sample → false high K (repeat if clinically unlikely, but treat if ECG changes). Forgetting glucose checks after insulin. Thinking calcium lowers potassium — it doesn't.

steps.title: Staging (KDIGO idea)
steps.body: AKI = creatinine rise ≥ 26.5 µmol/L (0.3 mg/dL) in 48 h, or ≥ 1.5× baseline in 7 days, or urine < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h. Stage by fold rise and urine output.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body:
- **Pre-renal:** hypovolaemia, sepsis, heart failure, NSAID/ACEi in dehydration.
- **Renal (intrinsic):** acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis, contrast, rhabdomyolysis.
- **Post-renal:** obstruction — prostate, stones, blocked catheter.

steps.title: Bedside first
steps.body: Check volume status, catheter flush, bladder scan, drug chart (stop nephrotoxins), urine dip, renal ultrasound for obstruction. Indications for urgent dialysis: refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, fluid overload, uraemic complications, certain toxins.

steps.title: Formulas
steps.body:
- **Corrected calcium (mmol/L)** = measured Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin g/L).
- **Calculated plasma osmolality** = 2×Na + glucose + urea (all mmol/L); normal ~275–295 mOsm/kg.
- **Osmolar gap** = measured − calculated; raised in toxic alcohols.

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: Ca 2.00, albumin 25 → 2.00 + 0.02×15 = 2.30 mmol/L (normal range). Na 150, glucose 30, urea 10 → 300 + 30 + 10 = 340 mOsm/kg — suggestive of a hyperosmolar state in the right context (HHS).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Correcting sodium too fast in chronic hyponatraemia (risk of osmotic demyelination) — follow protocol and senior advice.

steps.title: Recognise
steps.body: FAST: **F**ace drooping, **A**rm weakness, **S**peech difficulty, **T**ime to call 112. Note last-known-well time. Check glucose (hypoglycaemia mimics stroke).

steps.title: Pathway
steps.body: Urgent non-contrast CT (± CT angiography) to exclude haemorrhage. Ischaemic stroke within the licensed time window may be eligible for thrombolysis; large-vessel occlusion may be eligible for thrombectomy. Decisions are made by the stroke team using strict criteria. Aspirin is given only after haemorrhage is excluded and per timing protocol.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Not recording last-known-well time; lowering BP aggressively in ischaemic stroke without protocol; giving aspirin before CT.

scenes.text: Twenty fever patients in one morning OPD during the monsoon.

steps.title: Dengue (WHO 2009 framework)
steps.body: Febrile → critical (around defervescence, plasma leakage) → recovery. **Warning signs:** abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, clinical fluid accumulation, mucosal bleeding, lethargy/restlessness, liver enlargement, rising haematocrit with rapid platelet fall → admit. Avoid NSAIDs/aspirin; paracetamol for fever.

steps.title: Malaria
steps.body: Any fever in an endemic area: test (RDT or smear). **Severe falciparum** features: impaired consciousness, convulsions, respiratory distress, shock, jaundice, severe anaemia, hypoglycaemia, high parasitaemia, AKI → IV artesunate per national guidelines and HDU care.

steps.title: Enteric fever
steps.body: Stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, abdominal discomfort, coated tongue; blood culture early. Complications in the 2nd–3rd week: intestinal perforation, bleeding. Rising antimicrobial resistance — follow current national guidance.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Giving NSAIDs in dengue; relying on Widal alone; missing hypoglycaemia in severe malaria.

scenes.text: Under the microscope, some bacteria stain purple and others pink.
The difference lies in their cell walls.
Why does it matter? It guides the first antibiotic choice.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Cell wall
steps.body:
- **Gram-positive**: thick peptidoglycan, teichoic acids → retains crystal violet–iodine complex → **purple**.
- **Gram-negative**: thin peptidoglycan + **outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin)** → decolourised by alcohol → takes up safranin → **pink**.
- **Acid-fast** (mycobacteria): mycolic acids → resist acid–alcohol decolourisation after hot carbol fuchsin → **red** on blue background.

Other structures: capsule (antiphagocytic — pneumococcus), flagella, pili/fimbriae (adhesion; sex pili for conjugation), **spores** (Bacillus, Clostridium — very resistant), plasmids.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying endotoxin is secreted — it is part of the Gram-negative outer membrane (lipid A).
- Over-decolourising, which makes Gram-positives look Gram-negative.

scenes.text: You are given a sputum smear and asked to perform a Gram stain and a ZN stain.
Order matters — get it wrong and the result is wrong.
Put the steps in order.

steps.title: Gram stain
steps.body:
1. Make a thin smear, air-dry, heat-fix.
2. **Crystal violet** (primary stain) ~1 min.
3. **Gram's iodine** (mordant) ~1 min.
4. **Decolourise** with acetone/alcohol briefly.
5. **Safranin** (counterstain) ~1 min.
6. Wash, dry, examine under oil immersion.

steps.title: Ziehl–Neelsen
steps.body: Carbol fuchsin with heat (steaming) → 20–25% sulfuric acid (decolouriser) → methylene blue counterstain. AFB appear as red, slender, beaded rods. India's TB programme increasingly uses rapid molecular tests and fluorescence microscopy alongside smear.

steps.title: Safety
steps.body: Process TB samples in a biosafety cabinet and follow lab biosafety rules.

scenes.text: The hospital's central sterile services department receives instruments, gloves, culture media and plastic syringes.
Each needs the right method.

steps.title: Methods
steps.body:
- **Autoclave** (moist heat, 121 °C, 15 psi, ~15–20 min; or 134 °C for a shorter time): surgical instruments, linen, culture media. Biological indicator: *Geobacillus stearothermophilus* spores.
- **Hot air oven** (dry heat, 160 °C for 2 h): glassware, powders, oils, sharp instruments. Indicator: *Bacillus atrophaeus* spores.
- **Ethylene oxide**: heat-sensitive items (plastics, catheters, some equipment).
- **Ionising (gamma) radiation**: disposable syringes, gloves, sutures (commercial).
- **Filtration** (0.22 µm): heat-sensitive solutions (sera, antibiotics).
- **Disinfection**: glutaraldehyde (high-level, endoscopes), alcohol, chlorine (spills), povidone-iodine, chlorhexidine (skin).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing sterilisation (kills all forms incl. spores) with disinfection.
- Autoclaving oils or powders — steam cannot penetrate; use dry heat.

steps.title: Colour categories (Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016, as amended)
steps.body:
- **Yellow**: human anatomical waste, soiled dressings/cotton, expired or discarded medicines, chemical waste, microbiology lab waste (after pre-treatment).
- **Red**: contaminated recyclable plastics — tubing, catheters, IV sets, syringes without needles, gloves.
- **White (translucent, puncture-proof)**: sharps — needles, blades, scalpels.
- **Blue (cardboard box/container)**: glassware — broken or discarded glass, vials, ampoules.

Local hospital policy and the current rules always take precedence.

story.title: The cut finger and the measles shot

scenes.text: A cut is defended within minutes by neutrophils and complement.
A measles vaccine protects for decades because of memory cells.
Two arms of immunity.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: Two arms
steps.body:
**Innate**: barriers, phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), NK cells, complement, pattern-recognition receptors (TLRs) — immediate, no memory.
**Adaptive**: T cells (CD4 helpers — Th1, Th2, Th17, Tregs; CD8 cytotoxic) and B cells/plasma cells — specific, slower first time, **memory**. MHC I presents to CD8; MHC II presents to CD4.

steps.title: Antibody classes
steps.body:
- **IgG**: most abundant, crosses placenta, secondary response, opsonisation.
- **IgM**: pentamer, first antibody of primary response, best complement activator.
- **IgA**: secretory (dimer) in mucosa, breast milk.
- **IgE**: mast cells, allergy, helminths.
- **IgD**: on naive B cells.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Type I (immediate, IgE)**: mast cell degranulation — anaphylaxis, allergic rhinitis, asthma, urticaria.
- **Type II (antibody against cell/tissue antigen)**: transfusion reactions, haemolytic disease of newborn, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, Goodpasture, Graves' and myasthenia (receptor antibodies).
- **Type III (immune complex)**: serum sickness, SLE, post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis, Arthus reaction.
- **Type IV (delayed, T-cell)**: tuberculin (Mantoux) test, contact dermatitis (nickel), transplant rejection (acute cellular), granulomas.

steps.title: Key immunodeficiencies
steps.body:
- **X-linked (Bruton) agammaglobulinaemia**: BTK defect, no B cells, very low immunoglobulins; recurrent bacterial infections after maternal IgG wanes (~6 months).
- **DiGeorge syndrome**: 22q11 deletion — thymic hypoplasia (T-cell defect), hypocalcaemia, heart defects.
- **SCID**: severe T and B defects — infections from early infancy.
- **Selective IgA deficiency**: commonest; often mild; anaphylaxis risk with blood products.
- **HIV**: acquired CD4 T-cell loss.

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: Children with recurrent serious infections, failure to thrive or infections with unusual organisms should be referred to a paediatric immunologist. Live vaccines may be dangerous in some immunodeficiencies — the specialist decides.

steps.title: Vaccine types
steps.body:
- **Live attenuated**: BCG, oral polio (OPV), measles–rubella (MR/MMR), rotavirus, varicella, yellow fever. Strong, long immunity; generally avoided in pregnancy and severe immunodeficiency.
- **Inactivated/killed**: injectable polio (IPV), hepatitis A, rabies (cell culture).

- **Conjugate**: Hib, pneumococcal conjugate (PCV), typhoid conjugate.

scenes.text: A 30-year-old auto driver has had a cough for 3 weeks and lost weight.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: M. tuberculosis
steps.body:
Slender, acid-fast, slow-growing (weeks), obligate aerobe; spread by airborne droplet nuclei. Primary infection forms the **Ghon focus** (+ hilar nodes = Ghon complex); most infections become latent; reactivation often in lung apices.

**Diagnosis**: sputum smear microscopy (ZN or fluorescence), **rapid molecular tests** (cartridge-based or chip-based NAAT) that also detect **rifampicin resistance**, liquid/solid culture (gold standard, slow), line probe assays for drug resistance. Chest X-ray supports. Tuberculin test and IGRA detect infection, not disease.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using a positive Mantoux to diagnose active TB.
- Starting TB treatment without trying to obtain microbiological confirmation and drug-susceptibility testing.

steps.title: Salmonella Typhi / Paratyphi
steps.body:
Gram-negative motile bacilli; faeco-oral spread; invade via Peyer's patches. Clinical: stepwise fever, relative bradycardia, rose spots, splenomegaly; complications in week 3 (intestinal perforation, bleeding).

**Diagnosis**: **blood culture** is the investigation of choice in the first week (positive in a majority early); bone marrow culture is most sensitive; stool/urine culture later. **Widal test** (antibodies to O and H antigens) has poor specificity in endemic areas — a single titre is unreliable; a rising titre is more meaningful. Rising resistance to fluoroquinolones means treatment follows local sensitivity data.

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: Severe abdominal pain, bleeding, confusion or persistent fever beyond a week need hospital care. Prevention: safe water, hand hygiene, food safety and typhoid conjugate vaccine.

scenes.text: Pus from a boil and a throat swab from a child arrive at the lab.

steps.title: Key tests
steps.body:
- **Staphylococci**: Gram-positive cocci in clusters, **catalase positive**. *S. aureus* is **coagulase positive** (boils, abscesses, osteomyelitis, food poisoning with preformed toxin, toxic shock); *S. epidermidis* coagulase-negative (prosthetic devices).
- **Streptococci**: cocci in chains, **catalase negative**. *S. pyogenes* (group A, β-haemolytic, bacitracin sensitive): pharyngitis, cellulitis, rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis afterwards. *S. pneumoniae* (α-haemolytic, optochin sensitive, bile soluble): pneumonia, meningitis, otitis. *Enterococcus*: UTIs, endocarditis.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing α-haemolysis (green, partial) with β-haemolysis (clear, complete).
- Forgetting that rheumatic fever follows group A strep pharyngitis, not skin infection (skin infection is linked to glomerulonephritis too).

steps.title: Hospital-acquired infections
steps.body:
Common: catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI), central-line bloodstream infection (CLABSI), ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), surgical site infection. Organisms: MRSA, ESBL/carbapenem-resistant Gram-negatives (Klebsiella, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas), *C. difficile*.

**Bundles**: hand hygiene (WHO's 5 moments), maximal sterile barriers and chlorhexidine skin prep for line insertion, daily review of line/catheter need, head-end elevation and sedation breaks for ventilated patients, antimicrobial stewardship, environmental cleaning, isolation for multidrug-resistant organisms.

courses.summary: Virus structure and replication, HIV and its tests, hepatitis B serology, dengue, and malaria parasites — with case-based interpretation.

scenes.text: A 28-year-old comes for HIV testing after a risk exposure 2 weeks ago.
A negative test today may not be the final answer.
Why? Understand the virus and the window period.

steps.title: Learning note
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This study companion does not replace supervised clinical training, your faculty, or a licence to practise.

steps.title: HIV
steps.body: A retrovirus (RNA, envelope with **gp120** binding **CD4** and co-receptor CCR5 or CXCR4; gp41 fusion). **Reverse transcriptase** makes DNA; **integrase** inserts it into host DNA; **protease** matures new virions — all are drug targets. Transmission: sexual, blood, mother-to-child. Untreated infection → CD4 decline → opportunistic infections (TB, Pneumocystis, cryptococcus, toxoplasma, CMV) when CD4 falls below ~200 cells/µL.

steps.title: Testing
steps.body: Antibody tests, combined **antigen (p24) + antibody** tests (shorter window), and nucleic acid tests (viral load). The **window period** (time from infection to a positive test) depends on the test. India's national strategy uses a series of different rapid tests to confirm a positive result, with pre- and post-test counselling and consent. Treatment (ART) is offered to all diagnosed people; viral suppression prevents transmission.

steps.title: Help
steps.body: Free confidential testing and ART are available at government ICTC/ART centres. After a possible exposure, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) works best when started as early as possible — within 72 hours.

options: as soon as possible, within 72 hours

scenes.text: The liver clinic receives five hepatitis B serology reports.
HBsAg, anti-HBs, anti-HBc IgM/IgG, HBeAg.
Sort each into its meaning.

steps.title: Markers
steps.body:
- **HBsAg**: current infection (acute or chronic; > 6 months = chronic).
- **Anti-HBs**: immunity (after recovery or vaccination).
- **Anti-HBc IgM**: acute/recent infection (also in the 'window' when HBsAg has gone but anti-HBs not yet appeared).
- **Anti-HBc IgG**: past or chronic infection — **never** from vaccination.
- **HBeAg**: high replication/infectivity; HBV DNA quantifies it.

steps.title: Solved pattern
steps.body:
HBsAg −, anti-HBs +, anti-HBc − → **vaccinated**.
HBsAg −, anti-HBs +, anti-HBc IgG + → **recovered (natural immunity)**.
HBsAg +, anti-HBc IgM + → **acute infection**.
HBsAg + for > 6 months, anti-HBc IgG + → **chronic infection**.

lessons.title: Lab: Clinical case — fever in the monsoon (malaria vs dengue)

scenes.text: Monsoon brings many fever cases to the OPD.
Two patients: one with chills every other day, one with severe body ache and low platelets.
Test, identify and escalate.

steps.title: Malaria
steps.body: Female **Anopheles** mosquito injects sporozoites → liver (exo-erythrocytic) stage → red cells (erythrocytic schizogony) → gametocytes taken up by mosquitoes. *P. vivax* and *P. ovale* form **hypnozoites** (relapse; need primaquine radical cure after G6PD testing). *P. falciparum* causes severe malaria (cerebral malaria, severe anaemia, renal failure, ARDS) and shows **banana-shaped gametocytes**, multiple ring forms, high parasitaemia. Diagnosis: thick and thin peripheral smear (gold standard) and rapid diagnostic tests.

steps.title: Dengue
steps.body: Flavivirus spread by **Aedes** (day-biting). Fever, headache, retro-orbital pain, myalgia, rash; **warning signs** around defervescence: abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, mucosal bleeding, lethargy, liver enlargement, rising haematocrit with falling platelets. Tests: NS1 antigen (early), IgM (after about day 5). Management is supportive with careful fluids; avoid NSAIDs/aspirin.

steps.title: When to escalate
steps.body: Any warning sign in dengue, or any feature of severe malaria (confusion, convulsions, jaundice, low urine output, breathlessness), needs urgent hospital care.

s2.text: A second patient: day 4 of fever, abdominal pain, gum bleeding, platelets 40,000, haematocrit rising. Most likely?

choices.label: Dengue with warning signs — admit for monitoring and fluids
Simple viral fever; give ibuprofen
choices.feedback: NSAIDs increase bleeding risk in dengue.

end.text: Well done: P. falciparum identified, severe malaria escalated, dengue warning signs recognised.

steps.title: Vectors in India
steps.body:
- **Anopheles**: malaria.
- **Aedes**: dengue, chikungunya, Zika.
- **Culex**: lymphatic filariasis (Wuchereria bancrofti), Japanese encephalitis.
- **Sandfly (Phlebotomus)**: kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis).
- **Tsetse fly / reduviid bug**: African/American trypanosomiasis (not endemic in India).
- **Rat flea**: plague; **mite**: scrub typhus (Orientia).

steps.title: Control
steps.body: Source reduction (no stagnant water), bed nets, larvicides, indoor residual spraying, and community participation are core vector-control measures.

steps.title: Study companion only
