This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: History
steps.body: LMP and cycle regularity, obstetric history (gravida, para, previous complications), medical history (hypertension, diabetes, thyroid, epilepsy, heart disease), drugs (folic acid, teratogens), family history, social history, domestic violence screening asked privately.

steps.title: Investigations commonly offered
steps.body: Haemoglobin, blood group & Rh, blood sugar screening (per national guideline), urine routine/culture, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, thyroid where indicated, dating ultrasound; aneuploidy screening options counselled.

steps.title: Dating
steps.body: Gestational age = days since LMP ÷ 7. **Naegele's rule:** EDD = LMP + 9 months + 7 days (≈ LMP + 280 days) for a regular 28-day cycle. Early ultrasound (crown–rump length) dates more accurately.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Not starting folic acid; forgetting Rh status; missing high-risk factors that need specialist antenatal care.

steps.title: Routine
steps.body: Consent, chaperone, empty bladder, semi-recumbent with left tilt. Inspect (striae, scars, fetal movements). **Symphysis–fundal height** in cm roughly equals gestational weeks after ~24 weeks (± 2 cm). Leopold manoeuvres: fundal, lateral (lie and back), pelvic grips (presentation, engagement in fifths palpable). Auscultate fetal heart (normal baseline about 110–160 bpm).

steps.title: Refer when
steps.body: SFH much smaller/larger than dates (growth restriction, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy), non-cephalic presentation near term, reduced fetal movements, high BP or proteinuria.

steps.title: Definitions (WHO)
steps.body: Anaemia in pregnancy: Hb < 11 g/dL. Severity bands used in programmes: mild, moderate and severe (severe commonly < 7 g/dL).

steps.title: Approach
steps.body: Commonest cause iron deficiency; check MCV, ferritin, peripheral smear; consider folate/B12, haemoglobinopathies (thalassaemia trait — check partner), hookworm, malaria. Oral iron + folic acid; IV iron per guideline for moderate/severe or later gestation/intolerance; transfusion for severe anaemia with decompensation or near term per protocol.

steps.title: Escalate
steps.body: Severe anaemia, breathlessness at rest, heart failure signs, or near term → admit and involve the obstetric team; plan delivery at a facility with blood availability.

steps.title: Pre-eclampsia
steps.body: New hypertension after 20 weeks (≥ 140/90) with proteinuria or maternal organ dysfunction (renal, liver, neuro, haematological such as low platelets, HELLP) or uteroplacental dysfunction (FGR).

steps.title: Severe features
steps.body: BP ≥ 160/110, severe headache, visual disturbance, epigastric/RUQ pain, low platelets, raised liver enzymes, rising creatinine, pulmonary oedema.

steps.title: Principle
steps.body: Antihypertensives per protocol, magnesium sulphate for severe disease/eclampsia prevention, steroids for fetal lung maturity if preterm delivery likely, and delivery is the definitive treatment — timing decided by the obstetric team.

steps.title: Stages
steps.body:
**First stage:** onset of labour to full dilatation (latent then active phase; WHO 2018 recognises active phase from about 5 cm).
**Second stage:** full dilatation to delivery of the baby.
**Third stage:** delivery of baby to delivery of placenta and membranes.
(Some describe a fourth stage — first hour postpartum — for close monitoring.)

steps.title: Cardinal movements
steps.body: Engagement, descent, flexion, internal rotation, extension, restitution, external rotation, expulsion.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Unnecessary early interventions in the latent phase; not recording observations; not encouraging mobility and a companion of choice.

lessons.title: Lab: Partograph and CTG in words

scenes.text: Cervix 5 cm at 10 p.m.; 6 cm at 2 a.m.
Plotted on the partograph — it crosses the alert line.

steps.title: Partograph (classic WHO design)
steps.body: Records cervical dilatation, descent, contractions, fetal heart, liquor, moulding, maternal vitals, drugs. **Alert line** = expected 1 cm/h; crossing it → transfer/assess cause. **Action line** (4 hours to the right) → active intervention by a skilled team. Newer WHO Labour Care Guide uses time thresholds per cm.

steps.title: CTG in words
steps.body: Baseline rate, variability, accelerations, decelerations. Reassuring: baseline 110–160, variability 5–25 bpm, accelerations present, no concerning decelerations. Late decelerations (nadir after contraction peak) and reduced variability are concerning; prolonged bradycardia is an emergency.

steps.title: Remember
steps.body: CTG interpretation is in context: maternal fever, drugs, gestation. Escalate abnormal traces to the senior obstetrician.

scenes.text: A healthy baby is born. Now the most dangerous minutes for the mother begin.
AMTSL prevents postpartum haemorrhage.

steps.title: Components (WHO)
steps.body: Uterotonic (oxytocin is the recommended first choice) given within a minute of birth, controlled cord traction by a skilled attendant, uterine tone assessment (massage if needed) after placental delivery. Delayed cord clamping (not earlier than 1 minute) for newborn benefit when baby doesn't need resuscitation.

steps.title: Check
steps.body: Examine placenta and membranes for completeness, perineum for tears, estimate blood loss, monitor vitals and fundus regularly in the fourth stage.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Cord traction without counter-pressure on the uterus (risk of inversion); not examining placenta; under-estimating blood loss visually.

activity.prompt: Order AMTSL and immediate postpartum checks.

options: Not earlier than 1 minute after birth

scenes.text: Twenty minutes after delivery, the mother has lost about 800 mL, HR 118, BP 92/60.

steps.title: Definition & causes
steps.body: PPH: blood loss ≥ 500 mL within 24 h of birth (major ≥ 1000 mL). Causes — **4 Ts:** Tone (atony, commonest), Trauma (tears, rupture, inversion), Tissue (retained placenta), Thrombin (coagulopathy).

steps.title: Approach
steps.body: Call for help, ABC, two large-bore IV lines, bloods incl. crossmatch, fluids/blood, bimanual uterine compression and massage, uterotonics per protocol, IV tranexamic acid within 3 hours of birth (WHO), empty bladder, examine for trauma and retained tissue, escalate to balloon tamponade/surgery if unresponsive. Shock index (HR ÷ systolic BP) ≥ about 1 signals significant compromise.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Visual underestimation of loss; delaying help; forgetting to check for retained products and trauma when the uterus is firm.

steps.title: Suspect
steps.body: Any woman of reproductive age with abdominal pain, bleeding or collapse: **pregnancy test**. Risk factors: previous ectopic, PID, tubal surgery, IUD in situ, assisted conception, smoking. Shoulder-tip pain = diaphragmatic irritation by blood.

steps.title: Act

steps.title: Immediate steps
steps.body: Call for help, protect from injury, left lateral position, airway and oxygen, magnesium sulphate per protocol (loading then maintenance), control severe hypertension, monitor fetal heart, plan delivery once mother is stabilised. Monitor reflexes, RR, urine output; calcium gluconate is the antidote for magnesium toxicity.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using diazepam instead of magnesium as first choice; rushing to caesarean before maternal stabilisation; not monitoring for toxicity.

steps.title: Postpartum
steps.body: Eclampsia can occur up to several days postpartum; continue monitoring.

scenes.text: Two women bleed at 34 weeks: one painless bright-red bleeding, one with severe pain and a hard uterus.
Different diagnoses, different dangers.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body:
**Placenta praevia:** painless, bright-red, recurrent bleeding; soft non-tender uterus; malpresentation common. **Do not perform a digital vaginal examination** until praevia is excluded by ultrasound.
**Placental abruption:** painful, uterus tender and 'woody' hard, bleeding may be concealed — shock out of proportion to visible loss; fetal distress; coagulopathy risk.

steps.title: Management principles
steps.body: Resuscitate, crossmatch, coagulation screen, fetal monitoring, steroids if preterm, anti-D if Rh-negative, delivery decision by obstetric team.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Judging severity only by visible blood in abruption; performing a digital vaginal examination before ultrasound has excluded praevia; forgetting coagulation tests and anti-D.

steps.title: Avoid
steps.body: Pushing the cord back up; delay waiting for consultant to see it — call while acting.

steps.title: Risk factors
steps.body: Malpresentation, polyhydramnios, preterm, multiple pregnancy, artificial rupture with high presenting part.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: PALM-COEIN (FIGO)
steps.body:
**Structural (PALM):** Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma (fibroid), Malignancy/hyperplasia.
**Non-structural (COEIN):** Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not yet classified.

steps.title: Work-up
steps.body: History (pattern, intermenstrual/post-coital bleeding), pregnancy test, Hb, thyroid if indicated, pelvic ultrasound, endometrial sampling when age/risk factors indicate. Post-menopausal bleeding = urgent assessment for endometrial cancer.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Forgetting a pregnancy test; missing post-coital bleeding (cervical pathology); not treating the anaemia.

scenes.text: A 26-year-old, 6 weeks postpartum, breastfeeding, wants spacing.
Non-judgemental, informed choice.

steps.title: Options
steps.body:
- **Long-acting reversible (LARC):** copper IUD, levonorgestrel IUS, implant — most effective typical use.
- **Injectable (DMPA).**
- **Pills:** combined (avoid in early postpartum/breastfeeding per WHO MEC and in certain risks) and progestogen-only.
- **Barrier:** condoms (also protect from STIs).
- **Permanent:** tubectomy, vasectomy.
- **Emergency contraception:** levonorgestrel pill or copper IUD within the recommended window.

steps.title: WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria
steps.body: Categories 1–4 guide safety by condition (e.g. combined pills are not advised for migraine with aura, smokers ≥ 35, some cardiovascular risks). Use the current MEC chart rather than memory.

steps.title: Counselling principles
steps.body: Privacy, informed choice, no coercion, discuss effectiveness, side effects, return to fertility and STI protection.

steps.title: Screening

steps.title: Diagnosis
steps.body: Clinical: lower abdominal pain plus cervical motion, uterine or adnexal tenderness. Swabs for chlamydia/gonorrhoea, consider ultrasound for tubo-ovarian abscess.

steps.title: Treatment principles
steps.body: Start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics per national guidelines promptly (low threshold), analgesia, partner notification and treatment, abstinence until both treated, follow-up. Admit if severe, pregnant, tubo-ovarian abscess, or failing oral therapy.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Untreated PID → infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain. Handle confidentially and without judgement.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Describe systematically
steps.body: Patient, date, views (at least two, at right angles), bone and location (proximal/mid/distal, intra/extra-articular), fracture pattern (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted, segmental, greenstick/buckle in children), displacement (translation, angulation, rotation, shortening), open or closed (clinical), neurovascular status (clinical).

steps.title: Classic patterns
steps.body:
- **Colles' type:** distal radius fracture with dorsal displacement/angulation (dinner-fork).
- **Scaphoid:** anatomical snuffbox tenderness; may be invisible on initial X-ray — immobilise and re-image per protocol (risk of avascular necrosis).
- **Neck of femur:** shortened, externally rotated leg in an elderly patient after a fall.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Single view only; not imaging the joint above and below; dismissing snuffbox tenderness with a normal X-ray.

scenes.text: A 25-year-old: wound over the shin with bone visible, foot pulses present.
Open fracture = surgical emergency.

steps.title: Principles
steps.body: Primary survey first. Control haemorrhage, analgesia, **IV antibiotics as early as possible** per protocol, tetanus status, photograph the wound for records, remove gross contamination, saline-soaked dressing, splint/realign, neurovascular checks before and after, urgent orthopaedic (and plastic surgical) review for debridement.

steps.title: Gustilo–Anderson idea
steps.body: Grades by wound size, contamination and soft tissue damage; higher grades have greater infection and non-union risks.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Delaying antibiotics; repeatedly exposing the wound; forgetting tetanus; missing compartment syndrome (it can still occur with an open fracture).

steps.title: Distal neurovascular exam
steps.body: Colour, temperature, capillary refill, pulses; sensation in specific nerve territories; active movement of fingers/toes. Upper limb nerves: radial (wrist/finger extension, dorsal first web space sensation), median (thumb opposition/ thumb-index pinch, index pulp sensation), ulnar (finger abduction, little-finger sensation).

steps.title: Tight cast
steps.body: Increasing pain, swelling, numbness, poor capillary refill → elevate, split the cast down to skin (bivalve) and urgent senior review; consider compartment syndrome.

steps.title: Documentation
steps.body: Record before and after any manipulation or splinting.

steps.title: Study companion only

This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Differentials
steps.body: Septic arthritis (most urgent), crystal arthritis (gout, pseudogout), reactive arthritis, trauma/haemarthrosis, inflammatory arthritis flare.

steps.title: Act
steps.body: **Joint aspiration before antibiotics** (if this doesn't cause major delay): Gram stain, culture, crystals, cell count. Blood cultures. Then empirical IV antibiotics per protocol and orthopaedic referral for washout. Septic arthritis can destroy cartilage within days.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Assuming gout because of uric acid level (can be normal in acute gout and crystals don't exclude infection); starting antibiotics before aspiration without reason; injecting steroid into a possibly infected joint.

steps.title: Most back pain
steps.body: Is non-specific/mechanical and improves with staying active, simple analgesia and physiotherapy; imaging is not routinely needed.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body: Age < 20 or > 50 with new pain, history of cancer, unexplained weight loss, fever/immunosuppression/IV drug use (infection), significant trauma, osteoporosis/steroid use (fracture), night pain/constant progressive pain, bilateral or progressive neurological deficit, **saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction (cauda equina)**.

steps.title: Yellow flags

steps.title: Screening questions
steps.body: Pain or stiffness in muscles, joints or back? Can you dress yourself without difficulty? Can you walk up and down stairs?

steps.title: Examination
steps.body: Gait (symmetry, smoothness, turning), Arms (hands behind head, hands out, squeeze MCPs, grip, pinch), Legs (knee flexion, hip rotation, squeeze MTPs, inspect feet), Spine (inspect from behind/side, lateral flexion of neck, lumbar flexion).

steps.body: A simple table: G ✓ A ✓ L ✓ S ✓ with appearance/movement columns; abnormal findings trigger a detailed regional exam.

scenes.text: Your OPD has five back-pain patients and one has new bladder symptoms.

steps.title: Cauda equina
steps.body: Symptoms: bilateral sciatica, saddle/perineal numbness, urinary retention or incontinence, bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, reduced anal tone. Needs emergency MRI and decompression within hours when indicated.

steps.title: Safety-netting
steps.body: Give all back-pain patients written warning symptoms and advise to seek emergency care immediately if they occur.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Accepting 'some bladder change' without examination; delaying MRI to the next routine list.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: First aid
steps.body: Sit up, lean **forward**, pinch the soft part of the nose firmly for 10–15 minutes without releasing, spit out blood, ice on the bridge/cheeks optional. Check vitals.

steps.title: In hospital
steps.body: Assess ABC and blood loss, check anticoagulation/clotting, visualise with headlight, topical vasoconstrictor/anaesthetic, cautery of a visible anterior bleeding point (one side), anterior packing if not controlled; posterior bleeds → ENT for posterior packing/ further management.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Tilting the head back (blood swallowed, aspiration risk); pinching the bony bridge; stopping anticoagulant without considering clot risk — discuss with seniors.

steps.title: Rinne
steps.body: Fork on mastoid (bone conduction) then beside ear (air conduction). Normal/sensorineural: **AC > BC (Rinne positive)**. Conductive loss: **BC > AC (Rinne negative)** in the affected ear.

steps.title: Weber
steps.body: Fork on forehead/vertex. Normal: heard centrally. Conductive loss: lateralises **to the affected** ear. Sensorineural loss: lateralises **to the better (unaffected)** ear.

steps.title: Emergency
steps.body: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is an ENT emergency — urgent referral for assessment and time-sensitive treatment.

steps.title: Compare

steps.title: Inhaled foreign body

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Measure
steps.body: Each eye separately, with glasses if worn, at the chart distance (often 6 m). Record as distance/line read, e.g. 6/6 normal, 6/18 reduced. If < 6/6, repeat with a **pinhole**: improvement suggests refractive error. If unable to read top line: counting fingers, hand movements, perception of light.

steps.title: Children & illiterate adults
steps.body: Use E-chart or picture charts.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Testing both eyes together; forgetting glasses; not testing pinhole.

Record with/without correction

scenes.text: Five red eyes in one morning: sticky, gritty, painful with halos, photophobic, after a welding job.
Which can wait and which need same-day ophthalmology?

steps.title: Benign usually
steps.body: Conjunctivitis (discharge, normal vision, no pain), subconjunctival haemorrhage (painless, check BP and anticoagulation).

steps.title: Sight-threatening red flags
steps.body: Reduced vision, moderate–severe pain, photophobia, abnormal pupil, corneal opacity, halos with vomiting (**acute angle-closure glaucoma**), contact-lens wearer with painful eye (**microbial keratitis**), trauma/chemical. Refer same day.

steps.title: Key conditions
steps.body:
- **Acute angle-closure:** painful red eye, halos, fixed mid-dilated pupil, hazy cornea, very high IOP, nausea — emergency.
- **Anterior uveitis:** photophobia, ciliary flush, small pupil.
- **Keratitis:** pain, photophobia, corneal ulcer staining with fluorescein.

scenes.text: A 72-year-old: sudden painless loss of vision in one eye this morning.
Some causes are treatable only within hours.

steps.title: Causes
steps.body: Central retinal artery occlusion (sudden profound loss, pale retina with cherry-red spot — stroke-equivalent), central retinal vein occlusion ('blood and thunder' fundus), retinal detachment (flashes, floaters, curtain), vitreous haemorrhage (diabetics), ischaemic optic neuropathy — **giant cell arteritis** in > 50 with headache, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication.

steps.title: Act
steps.body: Urgent same-day ophthalmology. Suspected GCA: check ESR/CRP and start high-dose steroids promptly per protocol (to protect the other eye) while arranging confirmation. CRAO: treat as stroke — vascular work-up.

steps.title: Flashes and floaters
steps.body: New flashes/floaters or a shadow → retinal tear/detachment until proven otherwise; urgent dilated fundus exam.

story.title: Lime splash on the construction site

scenes.text: A construction worker gets wet cement/lime in his eye; screaming in pain.
Irrigation first — questions later.

steps.title: Why
steps.body: Alkalis (lime, cement, ammonia) penetrate deeply and cause severe damage; acids also injure. Outcome depends on how fast and how long you irrigate.

steps.title: Do
steps.body: **Immediate copious irrigation** with saline or clean water (topical anaesthetic helps), evert lids and remove particles, continue until pH of tear film is neutral (check with litmus after a few minutes' pause), then urgent ophthalmology review.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Waiting to test pH or for the doctor before starting irrigation; trying to neutralise with acid; not everting the upper lid.

steps.title: Structure
steps.body: Presenting complaint (often from caregiver), history of presenting illness, **antenatal, natal and postnatal history**, **developmental history** (four domains), **immunisation history** (card), **feeding/diet history**, family (consanguinity), socio-economic and home environment, school performance.

steps.title: Approximate milestones (vary between children)
steps.body:
- Social smile ~6 weeks; head control ~3–4 months.
- Sits without support ~6–8 months; transfers objects ~6 months.
- Pincer grasp ~9–12 months; stranger anxiety ~9 months.
- Walks independently ~12–15 months; first words ~12 months.
- Two-word phrases ~2 years.

steps.title: Red flags
steps.body: No social smile by 2–3 months; not sitting by 9 months; not walking by 18 months; no words by 16–18 months; **any loss of previously acquired skills (regression)** at any age; persistent primitive reflexes; asymmetry of movement.

steps.title: Tools

steps.title: Reading charts
steps.body: WHO growth standards (0–5 years) plot weight-for-age, length/height-for-age, weight-for-length/height and head circumference. Z-scores: below −2 = moderate, below −3 = severe deficit. **Underweight** = low weight-for-age; **stunting** = low height-for-age (chronic); **wasting** = low weight-for-height (acute).

steps.title: Faltering growth
steps.body: Crossing two major centile lines downwards needs assessment: intake, absorption (coeliac, CF), chronic infection (TB, HIV, UTI), psychosocial factors.

steps.title: Measure right
steps.body: Length lying down under 2 years, height standing after; calibrated scales; plot every visit.

lessons.title: Lab: Newborn resuscitation — the golden minute

scenes.text: A term baby is born limp and not breathing.
The first minute decides a lot.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: Initial steps (general, per current neonatal resuscitation programmes)
steps.body: Receive in a warm towel, **dry and stimulate**, keep warm, position the airway (neutral), clear secretions only if needed. If not breathing or gasping → **start bag-and-mask ventilation within the first minute**. Assess heart rate. If HR remains < 60/min despite 30 s of effective ventilation → chest compressions coordinated with ventilation (3:1) and call for advanced help.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Wasting time on routine suctioning; ineffective mask seal (check chest rise); letting the baby get cold.

steps.title: Thermal care
steps.body: Skin-to-skin, cap, delay bathing; hypothermia increases mortality, especially in low birth weight babies.

activity.prompt: Order the newborn resuscitation steps (general).
items: Receive baby in a warm, dry towel and note the time
Dry thoroughly and stimulate
Position airway; clear secretions only if necessary
If not breathing well, start bag-and-mask ventilation within 1 minute
Check heart rate and chest rise; correct ventilation technique
If HR < 60 despite effective ventilation, start chest compressions 3:1 and call advanced help

scenes.text: The midwife calls out observations at 1 minute.

steps.title: Components
steps.body:
**A**ppearance (colour): 0 blue/pale, 1 body pink extremities blue, 2 all pink.
**P**ulse: 0 absent, 1 < 100, 2 ≥ 100.
**G**rimace (reflex irritability): 0 none, 1 grimace, 2 cry/cough.
**A**ctivity (tone): 0 limp, 1 some flexion, 2 active.
**R**espiration: 0 absent, 1 weak/irregular, 2 good cry.

steps.title: Use
steps.body: APGAR describes condition at 1 and 5 minutes; **do not wait for the 1-minute APGAR to start resuscitation.**

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: Pink body/blue limbs (1), HR 120 (2), grimace (1), some flexion (1), weak cry (1) = 6.

scenes.text: Two babies: one yellow on day 1, one on day 4 but feeding well.
Timing separates physiological from pathological.

steps.title: Physiological vs pathological
steps.body: Physiological jaundice typically appears after 24 hours, peaks around day 3–5 in term babies, and resolves. **Pathological features:** jaundice within the first 24 hours, rapidly rising bilirubin, levels above treatment thresholds for age (hour-specific charts), prolonged jaundice (> 2 weeks term), conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia (pale stools, dark urine — think biliary atresia), unwell baby.

steps.title: Causes & treatment
steps.body: Haemolysis (Rh/ABO incompatibility, G6PD deficiency), sepsis, hypothyroidism. Treatment: phototherapy guided by hour-specific nomograms, exchange transfusion for very high levels; treat cause, support feeding.

steps.title: Danger
steps.body: Untreated severe hyperbilirubinaemia can cause kernicterus (bilirubin encephalopathy). Pale stools need urgent referral — early surgery in biliary atresia improves outcomes.

courses.summary: WHO dehydration plans, ORS and zinc, severe acute malnutrition criteria and refeeding principles.
outcomes: Learners can classify dehydration and choose Plan A, B or C

scenes.text: A 2-year-old with 8 loose stools a day for 2 days: irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, skin pinch goes back slowly.
Some dehydration — Plan B.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: WHO classification
steps.body:
**Severe:** two of — lethargic/unconscious, sunken eyes, drinks poorly/unable, skin pinch goes back very slowly (≥ 2 s) → Plan C (IV/NG).
**Some:** two of — restless/irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly/thirsty, skin pinch goes back slowly → Plan B (ORS in facility).
**No dehydration** → Plan A (home: extra fluids, ORS after stools, zinc, continue feeding).

steps.title: Zinc and ORS
steps.body: Low-osmolarity ORS plus zinc supplementation for 10–14 days (dose per age, per national guideline) reduces duration and severity. Antibiotics only for dysentery (blood in stool), suspected cholera with severe dehydration, or other specific indications.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: Using antidiarrhoeals in children; stopping feeding; prescribing antibiotics routinely.

activity.prompt: Classify each child.

items.text: Alert, eyes normal, drinks normally, skin pinch quick
Lethargic, unable to drink, skin pinch very slow

scenes.text: The 2-year-old weighs 12 kg and has some dehydration.
Plan B: about 75 mL/kg ORS over 4 hours.

steps.title: Plan B
steps.body: Give approximately **75 mL/kg** of ORS over 4 hours in the facility, in small frequent sips/spoonfuls; give more if the child wants and is passing stools. Reassess after 4 hours and re-classify (move to A, repeat B or move to C).

steps.title: Solved
steps.body: 12 kg × 75 = 900 mL over 4 hours ≈ 225 mL/hour.

steps.title: If vomiting
steps.body: Wait 10 minutes and continue more slowly; consider NG ORS if unable to drink.

activity.prompt: A 9 kg infant has some dehydration. Using Plan B (75 mL/kg over 4 h), total ORS volume?

story.title: The thin child at the anganwadi

scenes.text: A 2-year-old: very thin arms, swelling of both feet.
MUAC tape reads 11.0 cm.

steps.title: SAM criteria (6–59 months, WHO)
steps.body: Any of: **MUAC < 11.5 cm**, **weight-for-height < −3 Z**, or **bilateral pitting oedema**.

steps.title: Complicated vs uncomplicated
steps.body: Admit (inpatient/NRC) if medical complications, failed appetite test, or severe oedema. Uncomplicated SAM with good appetite may be managed in community programmes where available. Inpatient principles (WHO 10 steps idea): treat/prevent hypoglycaemia, hypothermia, dehydration (cautious, special ORS), electrolytes, infection (antibiotics), micronutrients, cautious start with low-energy feeds (F-75) then catch-up (F-100/RUTF), stimulation, prepare for follow-up.

steps.title: Refeeding & fluids
steps.body: Rapid feeding or IV fluids can cause heart failure and refeeding syndrome; follow SAM-specific protocols.

lessons.title: Lab: Capstone — child with diarrhoea at a CHC

scenes.text: Ravi has watery diarrhoea for 3 days, MUAC 12.2 cm, weight 9 kg, irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly.
Classify, treat, counsel.

steps.title: Integrated approach
steps.body: Check general danger signs (unable to drink, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargy). Classify dehydration, look for blood in stool, check nutrition (MUAC/weight), fever/malaria risk. Treat, counsel on feeding and when to return.

steps.title: When to return
steps.body: Many watery stools, repeated vomiting, marked thirst, eating/drinking poorly, fever, blood in stool, not getting better.

steps.title: Escalate
steps.body: General danger signs or severe dehydration → urgent treatment and referral.

s1.text: No general danger signs. Irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly. No blood in stool.

choices.label: Some dehydration — Plan B: 675 mL ORS over 4 h, start zinc
Severe — start IV fluids

courses.title: Paediatric emergencies
courses.summary: Paediatric assessment triangle, febrile seizures, respiratory distress, and paediatric fluid/weight calculations.
outcomes: Learners can use the paediatric assessment triangle
Learners can manage a febrile seizure and know when to investigate

scenes.text: From the doorway you see a floppy, grey child breathing fast.
Appearance, breathing, circulation — in seconds.

steps.title: Study companion only
steps.body:
This is for learning, not medical advice. For your own health, talk to a doctor or pharmacist. In an emergency call 112.

This course supports, but does not replace, supervised clinical training, local protocols and a medical licence.

steps.title: PAT
steps.body: **Appearance** (TICLS: tone, interactiveness, consolability, look/gaze, speech/cry), **work of breathing** (abnormal sounds, retractions, nasal flaring, positioning), **circulation to skin** (pallor, mottling, cyanosis). Abnormal appearance = brain/systemic problem; abnormal breathing alone = respiratory distress; abnormal all three = cardiopulmonary failure.

steps.title: Then ABCDE
steps.body: Follow the PAT with a hands-on ABCDE assessment and treat as you go. Check glucose ('don't ever forget glucose').

steps.title: Children compensate
steps.body: Hypotension is a late sign in children — tachycardia and delayed capillary refill come first.

activity.prompt: PAT finding → category.

items.text: Alert child, retractions and nasal flaring, pink skin
Lethargic, mottled skin, normal breathing effort

scenes.text: A 2-year-old with fever had a generalised seizure for 2 minutes at home; now drowsy but rousing.
Parents are terrified.

steps.title: Simple febrile seizure
steps.body: Age about 6 months to 5 years, generalised, < 15 minutes, single in 24 hours, full recovery, no CNS infection. Generally benign; find the fever source (otitis, UTI, viral).

steps.title: Complex or worrying
steps.body: Focal, > 15 minutes, recurrent within 24 h, incomplete recovery, meningism, very young age, or a seizure lasting > 5 minutes now → treat as status (benzodiazepine per protocol), and consider meningitis/encephalitis (LP per senior).

steps.title: Counsel parents
steps.body: Recurrence is common; place child on side, don't put anything in the mouth, time it, call 112 if > 5 minutes. Antipyretics help comfort but don't prevent febrile seizures.

s1.text: Generalised 2-minute seizure, now rousing, fever 39°C, no neck stiffness, ear drum red.

choices.label: Likely simple febrile seizure with otitis — treat source, observe, counsel parents
Start long-term antiepileptics
Order urgent MRI

s2.text: Next day a second seizure starts and is still going at 5 minutes.

choices.label: Treat as status epilepticus — ABC, oxygen, benzodiazepine per protocol, call senior
Wait until 30 minutes

end.text: Seizure stops after one dose. Senior evaluates; parents receive written seizure first-aid advice.

lessons.title: Lab: Noisy breathing — croup, bronchiolitis, asthma

scenes.text: Winter night: a barking cough, a wheezy 4-month-old, and a wheezy 7-year-old.
Same noise, different diseases.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body:
- **Croup:** 6 months–3 years, barking cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarse voice; steroid per protocol, nebulised adrenaline for severe stridor at rest.
- **Bronchiolitis:** under 1–2 years, RSV, coryza then cough, crackles/wheeze, feeding difficulty; supportive (oxygen if low, feeding support); bronchodilators/steroids generally not helpful.
- **Asthma:** usually older, recurrent wheeze, triggers, responds to bronchodilators.

steps.title: Don't miss
steps.body: Epiglottitis/bacterial tracheitis (toxic, drooling, sitting forward — don't upset the child, call anaesthesia/ENT), foreign body (sudden choking history), pneumonia.

steps.title: Admission signs
steps.body: Hypoxia, apnoea, poor feeding (< 50–75% usual), severe distress, dehydration.

story.title: The 18 kg child who can't drink

scenes.text: A 5-year-old, 18 kg, post-appendicectomy, NBM for 24 hours.
Write the maintenance fluid rate.

steps.title: 4-2-1 rule
steps.body: 4 mL/kg/h for the first 10 kg, 2 mL/kg/h for the next 10 kg, 1 mL/kg/h for each kg above 20. Use isotonic fluids with glucose per current guidance; monitor electrolytes, glucose and weight. Add deficit and ongoing losses separately.

steps.title: Hyponatraemia
steps.body: Hypotonic fluids have caused fatal hyponatraemia in children; isotonic maintenance fluid is generally recommended. Check sodium at least daily on IV fluids.
